Its cost cuts and 75% price pass-through target inflation, but whether margins hold as cable remotes keep shrinking remains an open question.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 25, 2026 at 12:51PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Universal Electronics ›

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 5, 2026, Universal Electronics (UEIC +4.76%) reported net sales of $89.4 million and reaffirmed its full-year earnings outlook. The company is restructuring operations and shifting focus toward smart home technology to counter shrinking demand for legacy television remotes.

Management cut non-GAAP operating expenses, which are adjusted figures excluding one-time items, by 20% year over year to align costs with flat sales. Lower overhead allowed earnings per share, or EPS, to rebound sharply from early-year losses.

Higher component costs and currency shifts squeezed gross margin, which measures profit after direct production expenses, down to 26.3%. Universal Electronics is passing these expenses to customers through price adjustments to protect margins.

Sales of traditional cable television remotes dropped as consumers cut subscriptions in favor of streaming services. Growth in heating, ventilation, and air conditioning, or HVAC, controls helped offset the decline in home entertainment hardware.

Universal Electronics relies heavily on internal operational discipline to navigate volatile supply chains and rising part costs. Management prioritizes forecast accuracy, working capital optimization, and inventory reductions while expanding partnerships with major climate control manufacturers.

Capital allocation stays focused on strengthening liquidity and paying down debt. The company reduced credit line borrowings while increasing cash balances, leaving it better positioned to fund high-margin smart home programs.

#3097. ElevenLabs is in early talks to raise at a $33B valuation, Bloomberg says

The voice AI company plans to start the round in early 2027, up 50% from its September valuation.

ElevenLabs is in early talks for a funding round at a $33B valuation, planned for the first quarter of 2027, Bloomberg reported. That would be 50% above its $22B valuation in September, and its annual recurring revenue has reached $700M, one person said.

ElevenLabs is in early talks to raise money at a $33B valuation, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter. The voice AI company plans to start the round in the first quarter of 2027, though some investors want it to begin sooner.

That would be a 50% jump from the $22B ElevenLabs was valued at in a $300M share sale in September. It also fits the company’s habit of setting valuations in multiples of 11, a nod to its name.

ElevenLabs’ annual recurring revenue has reached $700M, one person told Bloomberg, up from the $600M it reported in September. ElevenLabs declined to comment.

The price would be steep next to its peers. London video AI firm Synthesia was valued at $4B in January with about $140M in yearly revenue. Mistral was valued at €21B in September, having passed $400M early in the year.

Investors may be spurred on by Anthropic’s record $107.3B IPO, which brought early backers huge gains.

ElevenLabs was founded in London in 2022 by Mati Staniszewski and Piotr Dabkowski, and makes realistic AI voices for games, audiobooks and AI agents. Staniszewski has said it could start preparing for an IPO in 2028.

#3096. AirTag 2 has two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade

AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) launched earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade.

Precision Finding is Apple’s best AirTag feature, letting you get step-by-step, highly precise directions to your lost item. But with the original AirTag, you had to be in fairly close proximity before you could benefit from Precision Finding.

With AirTag 2, Apple added a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip that makes Precision Finding now available from up to 1.5x farther away than before. It’s a huge increase that I’ve definitely noticed.

This expansion of Precision Finding to greater distances means the feature is now available a lot more often than with the old AirTag. For this reason alone, I highly recommend AirTag 2.

When you’re trying to find a lost item, Precision Finding isn’t the only tool AirTag offers. There’s also a built-in speaker that can play a sound, triggered by your iPhone, to help you track it down.

With AirTag 2, Apple has made the built-in speaker 50% louder than before. The company says this enables hearing it from up to twice as far away.

I’ve been impressed by how loud the AirTag speaker is able to get now. Between the new speaker and upgraded Precision Finding, Apple has made AirTag 2 better in the ways that users are likely to care about most.

You can buy AirTag 2 for $18 on Amazon (regularly $29) for a limited time.

#3095. Ford Motor vs. Tesla: Which Automaker Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Ford's truck empire and commercial fleet business stand against Tesla's EV leadership and AI ambitions, with valuations that sharply diverge.

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 25, 2026 at 12:53PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Ford Motor Company ›

The battle for automotive dominance pits century-old manufacturing scale against high-tech electric innovation. Choosing between Ford Motor Company (F +1.72%) and Tesla Inc. (TSLA -0.89%) requires weighing established commercial strength against aggressive future-focused growth.

Ford relies on its dominant position in trucks and commercial fleets to fund its transition to electric vehicles. Tesla continues to lead the global market for electric vehicles while expanding into energy storage and artificial intelligence. These two companies represent very different philosophies on how vehicles should be built, sold, and powered for the next decade.

Ford Motor generates revenue by selling trucks, SUVs, and commercial vans through segments like Ford Pro and Ford Blue. It serves global retail, commercial, and government customers. This business is supported by a network of over 8,200 independently owned dealerships worldwide.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $187 billion. This represented a revenue decline of roughly 1.4% compared to the prior twelve-month period. During this same time frame, the company reported a net loss of about $7.8 billion, resulting in a net margin of roughly -4.2%.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, Ford Motor reported a debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 4.7x, a measure of total debt divided by shareholder equity. Its current ratio, measuring the ability to pay short-term bills, was roughly 1.1x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was approximately $12.5 billion.

Tesla operates a vertically integrated business model focusing on electric vehicles and sustainable energy products. The company sells vehicles directly to consumers and provides energy storage to residential, commercial, and utility customers. These operations span major markets across North America, Europe, and Asia.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue was about $103.6 billion. This reflects a revenue growth of approximately 8.3%. The company also reported net income of about $3.2 billion during this period, resulting in a net margin of approximately 3.1%.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, Tesla maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.1x, which indicates its total debt is very low relative to its shareholder equity. The current ratio, a measure of how easily a company can cover immediate bills, was close to 2.2x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, the company generated about $6.2 billion in free cash flow.

Ford Motor faces operational risks including supply chain disruptions and a reliance on specific battery component suppliers. The company also addresses quality control issues and recalls, including those related to NHTSA consent orders. Legal challenges include class action litigation over fuel pump defects and investigations into its BlueCruise driver-assistance technology.

Tesla remains dependent on a limited number of battery suppliers such as Contemporary Amperex Technology (CYATY -10.14%) and Panasonic. The company must successfully scale production for new products like the Robotaxi and Optimus robot to meet investor expectations. Legal and regulatory risks include pending lawsuits regarding its Autopilot and Full Self-Driving technologies.

Ford carries a lower Forward P/E, which relates stock price to future earnings estimates, and P/S ratio, comparing value to sales over the past twelve months, than Tesla.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

After a series of uninspired product launches like the Cybertruck, bulls contend the "Musk Magic" is back as the Elon Musk-led company unveiled its new Roadster in October. Investors are also feeling like there may be some magic in reported negotiations for Tesla to merge with Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.07%), the other publicly traded Musk-founded business.

Setting aside merger talk for the moment, Tesla, the business, has some challenges. Year-over-year sales are down about 9%, thanks to a combination of the elimination of EV credits in the Big Beautiful Bill of 2025 and possibly some personal animus toward Musk for his role early in the Trump administration. Still, Tesla is the leader in EV sales and is annually cited by Cars.com as the car made with the most American parts. The company also has a home electrification arm, primarily battery storage products like the Powerwall. For 2027, sales are expected to grow about 132% to $122 billion, with net income of about $8.2 billion.

Turning to Ford, the venerable U.S. automaker also has its challenges. The company has been losing market share for the past decade, now ranking third, behind General Motors Corp (GM +1.96%) and Toyota in U.S. car sales, with about 13% market share. The U.S. accounts for about 60% of Ford's sales.

While the company continues to build the Mustang EV, it has evolved to nearly a complete pickup truck and SUV lineup. Still, Ford aims to generate half of its sales volume from hybrids and EVs by 2030.

One potential game-changer: Ford announced in October the formation of Ford Energy to manufacture battery and energy storage systems for data centers and utilities. Those areas are seeing rising demand for storage, driven by AI and the continued importance of renewable energy in the U.S. power mix.

In 2027, sales should inch up $3 billion to about $180 billion, with net income rising $3.1 billion to $7.5 billion.

So which stock is the better buy? The matter is complicated by Tesla's potential merger with SpaceX. Expected to be an all-stock transaction, it is possible the merger could be pushed through at a valuation below current share prices, or at a premium that doesn't reflect the long-term profits one could make by owning stand-alone Tesla long-term.

Ford has its challenges, but the business remains an important industrial stock in the U.S., and its bargain-basement valuation makes it a good turnaround bet.

#3091. DocGo: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Overhead cuts and AI tools have cut DocGo's cost per in-home booking by over half, yet the company's path to profit still depends on shedding business.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 25, 2026 at 12:53PM EST

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 9, 2026, DocGo (DCGO +5.51%) announced a narrowed adjusted EBITDA loss--earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, adjusted for non-recurring expenses--of $3.2 million alongside revised full-year revenue guidance of approximately $300 million. Long-term investors should care because management is deliberately shedding unprofitable business lines to establish sustainable cash flow and reach profitability by year-end.

Three takeaways from the call explain how management plans to achieve that shift.

DocGo revised its top-line revenue guidance down to roughly $300 million as it shuts down unprofitable contracts. Winding down non-accretive operations, such as an Upstate New York medical transportation unit generating $10 million in annual revenue, helps clear a path toward positive earnings.

Corporate headcount reductions and automated software outreach reduced cost per booking by over 50% for in-home visits. Trimming selling, general, and administrative costs (SG&A), which cover corporate overhead, brings quarterly operating expenses down to $28.7 million.

Chief Executive Officer Lee Bienstock announced he will step down once a successor is named, after pivoting the company toward integrated care delivery. Board members are searching for operational leadership with turnaround experience to guide the next phase of expansion.

Operating losses are shrinking as third-quarter adjusted EBITDA improved to a loss of $3.2 million. The company benefits from mobile healthcare growth and lower transport overtime rates, while management focuses on disciplined pricing across core markets.

DocGo aims to complete its transition from emergency response toward integrated virtual and in-person care delivery.

#3090. Perplexity’s Time Machine lets AI agents search the web of the past

The tool arrives a day after a startup from xAI's co-founders launched a similar product for forecasting AI.

Perplexity’s artwork for its Time Machine API.

Perplexity has added Time Machine to its Search and Context APIs, letting agents see the web as it was up to 365 days ago so forecasting tests are not spoiled by hindsight. It follows Epochal’s Time Portal by a day, and Perplexity’s results come from its own tests.

Perplexity has launched Time Machine, a tool that lets AI agents search the web as it looked on a past date, the company said on Wednesday. It arrived a day after Epochal, a startup from three of xAI’s co-founders, launched a similar product.

Both target the same problem. An AI agent asked about a past election or earnings call can simply look up the result. That makes it hard to test how well it really predicts.

Time Machine adds a date cutoff to Perplexity’s search and page-reading tools for developers, so results come from copies saved before that date. Perplexity’s cutoffs reach back 365 days. Epochal says its archive spans more than 30 years.

Perplexity says it used the tool to train an AI model to forecast 2026 political events listed on Polymarket. In its own test, the trained model scored 0.80, just above the market’s 0.79.

It also says fewer of its pages leaked later information than rival Exa’s, at 0.25% against 1.10% in one test. That was judged by Perplexity’s own automated checker. Time Machine costs the same as Perplexity’s other API calls.

Web tools built for AI agents are multiplying. On the same day, Cloudflare began letting websites offer agents their own search.

Archives of the web are becoming contested ground. More than 241 news outlets now block the Wayback Machine to keep AI companies away from their old articles.

#3088. Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab CEO on How He Reached the C-Suite

Anthony Vetro’s journey from multimedia pioneer to executive

Kathy Pretz is the editor in chief of The Institute, IEEE's member publication

At the 2025 IEEE Vision, Innovation, and Challenges Summit, IEEE Fellow Anthony Vetro discusses the need for open innovation models to keep pace with rapid technological change taking place at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories.

The trajectory from researcher to top executive at a leading R&D organization doesn’t happen overnight. It took Anthony Vetro nearly 30 years to climb the corporate ladder at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass. He joined MERL in 1996, right out of college, and he has worked there ever since.

Vetro probably is best known for his research in multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.

Anthony Vetro Employer Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass.Title President and CEO Member grade FellowAlma mater Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school)

Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass.

Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school)

He became an IEEE Fellow in 2011 for his contributions to video coding, three-dimensional television, and multimedia adaptation.

Mitsubishi Electric has moved away from making televisions. It now focuses on developing systems including ones used for defense, electronics, the energy industry, and space exploration.

His ascension up the executive ranks began in 2018, when he was named a vice president and director of MERL. In 2023 he was appointed its president and CEO.

He also works closely with the company’s new U.S.-based innovation facility in Cambridge. And he recently took on a dual role as deputy head of Mitsubishi Electric’s global R&D activities, including in Asia and Europe.

Vetro credits IEEE with helping him develop his management skills after he served in several IEEE Signal Processing Society leadership positions. He also learned from his key roles in establishing international standards for digital image formats and video compression, he says.

“Between my IEEE activities, standards work, and some of the business shifts in Mitsubishi Electric, I eventually graduated to more management leadership roles,” he says.

Vetro is the son of immigrants. His father came to the United States from Italy and his mother from Sweden when they were both in their early 20s. They settled in New York City, on Staten Island.

Although neither parent went to college, his father stressed the importance of education to his son at an early age.

“My father started in the mailroom and worked his way up to eventually managing communication accounts and infrastructure for large financial companies,” he says. “My mother worked in banks, first as a teller and later doing bank reconciliation after pursuing some professional certifications.

“Through their jobs, they saw people with college degrees getting better positions and promotions, so education was something really ingrained in me.”

Vetro says he developed a passion for mathematics and engineering in middle school. He was accepted into the Staten Island Technical High School, a specialized pre-engineering institution. There he solidified his interest in pursuing a career in the field.

“A lot of students didn’t know what they wanted to major in at college, but I knew fairly early,” he says.

He was accepted into the accelerated bachelor’s and master’s engineering degree programs at the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school). He began his bachelor’s degree program in 1992 and the master’s program in 1994.

“As part of the master’s degree program, I needed to do a thesis,” he says. “I wasn’t sure exactly what it would be on. Soon after taking my first course on image processing, I was certain that was an area I wanted to work in.”

It was an interesting time, he says, because broadcast television was going through a major transformation, shifting from analog to digital during the early 1990s. It was long before streaming services, he notes.

“I feel that industry-level engagement in IEEE is very vital to the organization in maintaining high relevance in the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity.”

“The idea of being able to come up with compact ways to represent this very rich information was really appealing to me,” he says. “I’m also a visual learner. I liked seeing images, and there was some nice math behind them, too.”

After he earned both degrees in 1996, Mitsubishi Electric hired him for its technical staff. He conducted research on multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.

“The opportunity to work on projects around digital TV broadcasting and image processing attracted me,” he says.

He conducted research in video conferencing, Internet and mobile streaming, and video coding technology, widely used for broadcasting, DVDs, and Blu-ray discs. He developed several technologies including digital TV receivers and displays, surveillance and camera-monitoring systems, automotive equipment, and satellite imaging systems.

Another advantage of joining the company, he says, was that it allowed him to pursue a doctorate in electrical engineering, also from Polytechnic, while working.

“That really sealed the deal,” he says. He received the degree in 2001.

After six years as a technical staff member, he was promoted in 2007 to manage the group working on digital video coding, processing, and streaming. Seven years later, Vetro became its deputy director, a top-level management position that he held until 2018.

“After working for about 10 years exclusively on video compression processing technology, there were some shifts in our company’s business. Its overall strategy began to change,” he says, “so I became interested in broadening my experience beyond video.”

He was asked to lead the lab’s speech and audio team. It was more development-oriented, he says, and focused on vehicle infotainment and speech interfaces before Alexa and Siri existed. He pivoted the team’s focus more toward research and established strategic paths tailored to emerging opportunities within the organization. Recognizing emerging trends in sensing and information security, he formed groups that worked on them.

To help spur innovation between Mitsubishi Electric and its U.S. customers, the company in June opened Serendie Street Boston, its first digital transformation hub in the United States. It’s colocated with MERL.

The new office is modeled after the first Serendie Street collaboration space, which Mitsubishi Electric launched in 2024 in Yokohama, Japan.

The word serendie is a combination of serendipity and digital engineering, according to the company’s website. Serendie is the digital platform designed to foster collaborations between data, people, and technology, it says. The space where people interact to extract ideas from the data is called “the street.”

The platform brings together researchers, startups, customers, and partners to identify new products, test them, run pilot programs, and scale them up.

Vetro says he’s excited about the endeavor.

“Serendie Street [Boston] aims to strengthen the bridge between our global R&D efforts and real-world industry challenges. The hub is intended to bring our partners and customers together to engage in more cocreation activities, where we listen to their problems and work together to solve them,” he says. “I think the company has come to recognize that we can’t just do it all internally by ourselves.”

The technologies being worked on include robotics, energy solutions such as integrating renewable energy into the grid, and more energy-efficient data center systems.

The decision to colocate the hub with MERL offices was deliberate, Vetro says.

“The area has a very rich ecosystem,” he says. “We have Harvard, MIT, and many other universities a stone’s throw away.”

Vetro joined IEEE in 1992 as a student member during an event the Polytechnic’s student branch was holding. He enjoyed reading the IEEE Potentials student member publication and other periodicals, he says.

“In the earliest stages of my career, IEEE was a place where I could attend conferences, read journals, and stay on top of the latest research and trends,” he says. “Over the years, I was able to build a professional network, which has been helpful. That facilitated a lot of research collaboration with university professors attending the conferences.

“In more recent years, IEEE has provided a great platform for industry to exhibit thought leadership and discuss real-world problems we’re facing. I think these discussions may have even set some research directions among the academic community.”

Vetro is an active volunteer for the IEEE Signal Processing Society. He has chaired several of its technical committees and conferences, and he served as an associate editor for some of its journals.

He says he’s most proud of establishing the society’s industry board and serving as its inaugural chair. The board formed a corporate engagement program, launched the Industry Signals newsletter, developed short courses tailored to industry, and holds career fairs at the society’s flagship conferences.

Vetro also had a hand in MERL sponsoring two IEEE technical field awards: the Flanagan Speech and Audio Processing Award and the Fourier Award for Signal Processing.

“Industry-level engagement in IEEE is really very vital to the organization in maintaining its relevance to the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity,” he says.

Kathy Pretz is editor in chief for The Institute, which covers all aspects of IEEE, its members, and the technology they're involved in. She has a bachelor's degree in applied communication from Rider University, in Lawrenceville, N.J., and holds a master's degree in corporate and public communication from Monmouth University, in West Long Branch, N.J.

#3086. New Gemini setting lets you keep chat history, but turn off AI training [U]

Update 11/24: This new setting is now widely rolling out. On gemini.google.com, tap the settings gear icon to find a new “Gemini History” item at the very bottom. This opens myactivity.google.com/product/gemini with an On/Off dropdown.

Under “Help train generative AI models with,” you’ll find the new “Chat content including text & attachments” setting. It’s enabled by default.

Your future chats won’t be used to train generative AI models, unless you provide feedback.

Training on “Audio and Gemini Live videos & screenshares” remains an opt-in preference.

Original 11/16: Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”

Google is now separating that preference into two new options.

This is huge. One of the major things Siri-AI users on iPhone like to point out is that while their assistant is a less capable portmanteau of Siri and Gemini, their queries are not used for AI training. Gemini on Android, on the other hand, offers the superior AI platform with the caveat that there is no way to opt out of training and still retain your chat history. Until now. Now users of Gemini on Android get the best of both worlds - the best of Google's AI models powering their AI experiences and their chat history siloed from AI training.

The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled:

“…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers.”

The duration is currently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, users, and the public.

The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.”

With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.

If Keep Activity is currently off, the two “new settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying users via email.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every November, I commit an act of subscription arson. Netflix? Cancelled. HBO Max? Gone. Disney+, Hulu, Apple TV? Cleared out like a fridge before vacation. Then, just as the Black Friday streaming deals start rolling in, I sign right back up, at a fraction of the price. It's the closest thing to a financial magic trick that doesn't involve a crypto wallet, and it works every single year.

The problem it solves is real. A Tom's Guide survey about streaming habits found that readers are spending more than $60 a month on seven or more streaming services. That's a lot of money to spend on a pile of apps you open just to scroll for 20 minutes before rewatching "The Office." Prices keep creeping up, and your watchlist isn't getting any shorter.

I prefer to play musical subscriptions instead: Cancel the ones I'm not using, hop back in when a sale comes along. Below, I'll walk you through exactly how I do it and round up seven streaming deals worth grabbing before they vanish.

At $4.99 a month for an entire year, this Disney+/Hulu bundle is almost absurdly cheap. One subscription gets you two major streaming libraries, from Hulu hits like “Only Murders in the Building” to Disney+ movies, series and family favorites. Frankly, it's hard to argue with that kind of entertainment bargain.

HBO Max sits at No. 1 in our best streaming services rankings, and for good reason. Its lineup is stacked with acclaimed shows like "The Pitt" and "A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms" and all-time great dramas including "The Sopranos" and "Veep," plus a deep bench of movies from Warner Bros. It's a one-stop shop for seriously good TV and film.

Apple TV is getting a serious Black Friday price cut, dropping to just $6.99 per month instead of its regular $14.99. It's a great, cheaper way to catch buzzy series like "Slow Horses," "The Studio" and "Silo."

Paramount+ is discounting both subscription tiers for Black Friday, but the Premium plan is the one worth splurging on. It includes everything in Essential, with the added bonus of Showtime's lineup of movies and series, a live feed of your local CBS station and mostly ad-free streaming. That's a lot of extra bang for your subscription buck.

If you're a "Walking Dead" completist, AMC+ is practically essential. The service has the original zombie saga alongside spinoffs like "Daryl Dixon." This Prime Video channel deal makes it a perfect excuse to revisit the franchise or finally catch up on all the undead drama.

BritBox is a streaming paradise packed with British television from the BBC and ITV. Its library spans generations of acclaimed mysteries, juicy dramas, offbeat comedies and fascinating documentaries. This is the perfect deal if you want to catch the upcoming "The Other Bennet Sister" three-part Christmas special.

The workaround is almost insultingly simple: Sign up with a different email address.

You likely have a spare lying around already, probably the one you made in 2011 and now use exclusively for receipts. If not, any of the many email services with a free tier will do the trick, whether that's Gmail, Yahoo, Outlook or AOL.

Here's my annual routine. Last year, Past Me, a surprisingly responsible person, set calendar reminders to cancel everything I signed up for during Black Friday week. Then I take my fresh email address and go deal hunting. The ones I think are worth your money every year are Peacock, HBO Max and Paramount+.

A word of warning: Some of the best deals out there are for annual plans, which means you can't churn them month to month. But the discounts are steep enough that paying upfront is still the smarter play.

And whatever you do, set a reminder to cancel next year. Future You will thank you.

In a word: no. Netflix doesn't do Black Friday. I check every year, and every year I'm met with the same cold, red-logoed silence.

Netflix has rarely discounted its plans, and Black Friday and Cyber Monday are no exception. So the usual monthly prices stand: $8.99 for Standard with ads, $19.99 for Standard ad-free, and $26.99 for Premium with 4K Ultra HD.

The upside of having no deal to chase is that you're not locked into a discounted annual plan, which makes Netflix the easiest service on the list to churn. Netflix knows this, of course, and has gotten sneaky about it. Its biggest shows now tend to arrive in installments, a neat little trick for making sure you stick around for the next drop.

#3084. Prediction: SpaceX Stock Will Be Worth This Much in 3 Years

It's down from its first-day closing price, but it has lots of room to grow.

By Jennifer Saibil – Nov 25, 2026 at 1:00PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›

Anthropic has dethroned Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.07%) as the largest initial public offering (IPO) ever, but SpaceX is off to a great start as a public company. Revenue is growing fast, and the company's first quarter as a public company was also its first quarter with a net profit.

SpaceX has three segments, all in rapidly changing, revolutionary industries, so the company could look very different in three years. Here's what could happen.

SpaceX gets its name from its space business, which is the world's largest rocket-launching company. It works with private companies, as well as government agencies like NASA, and it brings satellites into space for its Starlink broadband business.

The company measures its progress by launches and mass to orbit in tons. It has already launched 113 rockets this year as of the end of the third quarter, sending 1,517 metric tonnes into space, and its business represents 90% of global mass to orbit. Revenue increased 6% year over year to $1.8 billion in the quarter, and it reported an operating profit last year but a $7 million loss this year. As it scales, it's likely to become reliably profitable.

CEO Elon Musk announced a new base opening in Louisiana, set to launch in 2029. It's going to have 20 launch towers, and he expects it to launch thousands of rockets annually into space, bringing millions of tons of cargo. While there should be high capital expenditures to get it up and running, SpaceX just caught its first landing spaceship, and reusable rockets should dramatically lower its costs.

Starlink is growing fast and highly profitable. It offers satellite broadband across the globe and currently covers 174 countries. It has more than 11,000 satellites in low earth orbit, and it plans on having 100,000, covering every area of the world, including lakes, oceans, and airplanes. It has 13.6 million customers as of the end of the third quarter, up from 12 million the year before, and it already has deals with many of the world's major airlines.

Revenue increased 69% year over year to $5.2 billion in the third quarter, and operating income doubled to $2.4 billion.

The artificial intelligence (AI) business xAI merged with SpaceX earlier this year before the IPO, and the company renamed it Superintelligence (AI). It fits with the other segments because management expects to launch a million mini, solar-powered data center satellites into space, and AI is where management sees its biggest opportunities.

So far, it's growing fast. Revenue increased 830% year over year in the third quarter, but that included revenue from the acquisition of the coding company Cursor, so growth may slow. Operating income swung from a $1.7 billion loss to $431 million.

The company now has two huge data center clusters, Colossus I and II, with I fully rented to Anthropic. It has 1.7 gigawatts of power, and it expects to have 2.5 to 3 by the end of the year. Musk thinks it will have another 10 by the end of 2027, and possibly 20.

It also has its own AI model, Grok, and its AI agent, Grok bot, of which Musk said, "I've never seen anything grow this fast."

Here's where it gets a bit tricky. Even if everything goes smoothly and SpaceX is much bigger in three years, its stock may not take off quite the same way. That's because it's already extremely expensive, trading at 55 times trailing 12-month sales. That kind of valuation isn't likely to last.

Wall Street expects revenue to increase 272% in 2027, a major acceleration from the third quarter's 161%, and earnings per share of $0.34. Elon Musk said he thinks annual recurring revenue could reach $500 billion to $1 trillion next year, implying a much larger increase from today's $32.7 billion in trailing 12-month revenue.

Regulations could also potentially change, slowing down AI development in general and impacting SpaceX.

Let's suppose it can grow by a compound annual growth rate of 80% over the next three years. That would generate $190 billion in revenue over three years. At just under half of today's price-to-sales ratio, 25, the market cap would be $4.8 trillion, or about 260% higher than today's price.

#3081. Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026, plus more AI workplace updates

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The company also released new ROI tracking tools for companies monitoring their AI spend.

AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption. Microsoft has just put its offering into the ring.

During the keynote for the company’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella announced Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities.

Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost

The product, available in Frontier for now, is similar to OpenAI’s ChatGPT Space and several new Anthropic features, including Whiteboard and Sheets, which essentially merge the work tools you’re used to using with an agentic framework.

“As the evolution of Copilot Notebooks, it’s where people and agents build on each other’s work,” Microsoft said. “An agent drafts a section of a document, and you review. You leave a comment, and an agent picks it up.”

Microsoft also announced Autopilot, a sort of counterpoint agent to Copilot that “can watch Teams channels, follow up on emails, run recurring work, and manage a project — without waiting for a prompt,” as Microsoft described.

In a demo video during the keynote, the agent appeared to function similarly to OpenAI’s Dots, but for work — employees can tag their Autopilot “like a colleague,” Microsoft said, and assign it tasks.

Also: 4 ways Anthropic’s new Claude Sheets beat using a Google Sheets connector

Microsoft said the agent will be able to autonomously handle “meetings and follow-ups on its own,” though that claim may be best verified by teams themselves.

Speaking of trust, however, Microsoft noted that “Autopilot runs on the identity, security, and compliance foundation IT already uses,” and that “each Autopilot has its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID and a named manager,” meaning IT can block it as needed.

“Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail. Powered by Work IQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions,” Microsoft said.

The company added that employees will soon “be able to bring their personal Autopilot into Workspaces” as well. The feature is also available in Frontier.

Nadella also announced a few other productivity features, including a “command center” called Today that spans email, calendar, meetings, tasks, and threads in Teams. Currently in private preview in Outlook and the Copilot app, it includes a personalized briefing and a feed of priorities that updates throughout the day.

“The draft is written and ready for you to edit; the schedule change is already proposed; and the forgotten follow-up is waiting for you to send it, complete with context so you can catch up quickly,” Microsoft said of the feature, which sounds like an agentic briefing-cum-morning-assistant.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill

Microsoft also announced that Home, now generally available, unifies Chat and Cowork into a singular starting point. That’s similar to Anthropic’s recent consolidation of its chat and agentic Cowork offerings, demonstrating an overall trend toward simplification in workplace AI.

While more companies are finally starting to see a return on their AI investment, agents are still expensive and can quickly rack up costs when unsupervised.

Microsoft announced a few tools to track this at Ignite: Agent 365 Business Analytics and Agent 365 Cost Management.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Agent 365, which Microsoft announced last year, is the company’s observability platform. Microsoft said Business Analytics, in Frontier Public today, provides insights on what a company is spending on AI and why, and where it’s paying off, as well as forecasts future costs. In a demo during the keynote, Microsoft showed how admins can see when specific agents’ costs have spiked recently and what (human) employee to notify as a result.

“It starts with a new way to measure your investment: in work completed, not simply tokens,” Microsoft said. “It analyzes the tasks, how long that work typically takes a person, and the share Cowork performed, providing a sophisticated view of the hours your intelligence supports and what the work is worth.”

Cost Management lets IT see where teams are using AI down to the model.

“Leaders can set spending policies, limits, and proactive alerts and control which models are available,” Microsoft said. Anthropic released a similar tool last month, though it was focused more on making seats as efficient as possible on Teams and Enterprise plans.

#3080. Apple Mail added four convenient new features in iOS 27

iOS 27 brought new features to Apple Wallet, Maps, Notes, Messages, and more—and it includes key upgrades for the Mail app too. Here’s everything new for Apple Mail in iOS 27.

Suggestions at the top of messages have been in Apple Mail for years. But in iOS 27, they have a new, more flexible design and expand to support third-party apps.

In iOS 27, third-party apps can offer suggestions too. And when multiple apps are available with suggested actions, there’s a drop-down menu to show you all available options.

The retail giant partners with Meta to bring AI-powered shopping to the holiday season

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Black Friday shopping can be exhausting, especially when you're juggling multiple wish lists, comparing prices and trying to stick to a budget. But this year, Walmart is giving shoppers the option to hand some of that work over to AI.

On Tuesday, Walmart announced a partnership with Meta that lets customers shop its Black Friday deals through Muse, Meta's personal AI agent.

Unlike traditional AI chatbots that recommend products and send you links, Muse can take you through the purchasing process without leaving the conversation. Of course, you'll still have to actually approve the purchase, but it could be helpful when time is of the essence.

And if you're nervous about giving AI access to your credit card, Walmart has built in some safeguards.

Let's say you're looking for a blender but you don't want to spend your entire afternoon comparing models. You can tell Muse what you're looking for, how much you're willing to spend and whether you need it delivered.

Walmart handles the product matching behind the scenes through its new Agent Gateway.

According to the retailer, shoppers will have access to the same prices available on Walmart.com, including Black Friday discounts and applicable membership benefits.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Walmart also says the integration doesn't expose your broader shopping history to third-party agents.

I decided to give this a try (hopefully my husband isn't reading this). I started by simply heading to Muse.ai. From there, I described what I wanted. You can be as descriptive as you want or even vague. I simply gave the prompt, "My husband does a lot of yard work and I'd like to find a gift to help make the job easier." I didn't give a budget (it prompted me "what's your budget?) or any other specific requirements, but you can up front to make shopping even more personal and streamlined. Once you've done that, you're going to want to do the following:

Connect your Walmart account. Muse will direct you to Walmart to sign in before returning you to the conversation.

Set your spending limit. When adding your first product, you'll create a Walmart Agent Profile to manage what the AI is authorized to do.

Complete your purchase. You can check out directly through the conversation with your existing Walmart payment method.Muse showed me a few items before completing the purchase. Rest assured it does pause so you can see the choices. My husband has many of the items on the list already, so that hesitation was appreciated. Since my credit card is already connected to Walmart, this safeguard is important. The last thing I want is to spend hundreds of dollars on yard equipment we already have!

Walmart's regular return policy still applies to purchases made through Muse.

The more specific you are about what you need, the more useful AI shopping could be. If you're looking for someone on your list who is difficult to shop for like a teenage boy, this Muse partnership could be a lifesaver. Here are five prompts worth trying.

"Find me the best Black Friday deal on a 55-inch 4K TV under $300 at Walmart."

"Help me buy Christmas gifts for three kids ages 6, 9 and 12 with a total budget of $150."

"Find five tech gifts under $25 that are currently discounted at Walmart."

"Find the best Black Friday deals on wireless headphones under $100. Prioritize battery life and noise cancellation."

"Help me find stocking stuffers for four people without spending more than $50 total."

I'd recommend including instructions to show you the individual prices and total cost before completing any purchase.

Between shopping lists, crowded stores and seemingly endless Black Friday sales, there's certainly an appeal to having AI take care of some of the legwork.

But I'd still recommend double-checking product specifications, customer reviews and prices at competing retailers before letting an AI agent make a purchase. Just because something is discounted doesn't necessarily mean it's the best deal.

Walmart says it plans to bring its shopping experience to additional AI agents and apps in the future. For now, Muse offers another way to tackle your holiday shopping list without opening dozens of browser tabs.

#3078. Microsoft’s new Licensed Weights lets businesses customize AI models with their own data

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Microsoft is bridging the gap between proprietary and open-weight AI while targeting data-conscious businesses.

During the keynote at its Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced several new models from Microsoft AI (MAI), its lab within the company. But new model releases are almost a dime a dozen these days, and accelerating fast — what really stood out was how Microsoft will let its customers access those models.

Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5

MAI said it would allow its customers to customize its frontier models with their own data and run them securely in Azure through an initiative called Licensed Weights. It’s essentially a selective approach to open-weight AI: more so than proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic, but not fully downloadable on Hugging Face like Mistral’s Le Chonk. Interested companies will need to go through their Microsoft account reps to get started.

“You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay entirely yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents,” Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of MAI, said during the keynote.

The approach should stand out to businesses looking for affordable AI that lets them retain control over their IP. Microsoft said it would only use customers’ information to train its models if they agreed.

“No one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model,” Suleyman said during the keynote, a nod to an argument Palantir CEO Alex Karp has made repeatedly.

The dominant, if simplified, narrative in AI has been that proprietary, expensive models boast peak capabilities but aren’t customizable, while open, cheaper models are customizable but less capable. Microsoft’s AI models don’t necessarily compete with OpenAI and Anthropic yet, but the company has legacy sway with countless businesses. By offering a customizable AI option, it could strike a balance among major tech companies.

Western labs, including Thinking Machines and Mistral, are releasing more competitive open-weight models, but Anthropic and OpenAI still have the overwhelming majority of the enterprise AI market. Though Licensed Weights isn’t an open-weight family of models, it does diversify the open-versus-closed debate a bit and differentiate Microsoft’s offering from OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s. It’s also a smart pairing with Microsoft’s goal to balance price and performance, if businesses find it impressive enough.

Also: Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026

“Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at just 40% of the cost, and against Opus 5.5 it’s an incredible 5% of that cost,” Suleyman said of the new coding model the company announced at Ignite.

The company also released its new image editing model, MAI Image 2.7, on Tuesday, which now leads the category on Artificial Analysis while beating Nano Banana Pro and several GPT image models on price and quality. With Licensed Weights, Microsoft has positioned itself for organizations seeking a reliable blend of ROI tools, customization, security controls, and capability.

#3075. I’ve tested Ubuntu 27.04 ahead of its April release – and it will wow you

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

I've been using Ubuntu 27.04, and the speed boost is noticeable. Here's what else is coming.

Ubuntu 27.04, Tenacious T-Rex, is set for an April 22, 2027 release. Although that seems a long way off, it’s sooner than you think. As is implied by the release number, 27.04 is not an LTS release, so it only receives support for nine months (until January 2028). The good news is that you can migrate from 27.04 to 27.10, and then to the LTS release, 28.04. The entire upgrade path ensures that you don’t have to miss a single release.

But what’s coming in Ubuntu 27.04? Given that it’s an interim release, you’re probably assuming that there’ll be nothing exciting to be found. Although there won’t be any game-changing additions, there will be plenty of refinements and bug fixes.

Also: I’ve used Ubuntu for 22 years – and 26.10 might be its best release yet

I’ve been using the daily release of Ubuntu 27.04 for a bit. Let’s take a look at what is currently expected in Tenacious T-Rex.

This is probably the biggest addition to the next release of Ubuntu. And although you won’t find any major changes in GNOME, there are some important ones. First off, there will be editable quick settings, which allow for customizing, adding, removing, and rearranging toggles and widgets. GNOME 52 will also enjoy a revamped calendar popover, which streamlines the feature to focus primarily on events, time, and weather.

Also: Over Ubuntu? Fedora is the Linux distro I’d hop to next – here’s why

There will also be several improvements to window management, such as a spatial overview and a mosaic/tiling system for auto-resizing and organizing windows, a refined full-screen Alt+Tab app switcher, which will be capable of grouping older windows by application while showing newer ones individually, and finally, the ability to remember window sizing, placement, and workspace.

Desktop search is also getting a bit of polish by way of a redesigned popover and an improved results overlay that includes file previews, multiple actions, and search filters. And, as usual, there will be plenty of bug fixes and performance enhancements. The bump in speed is noticeable, too, in my testing.

Ubuntu 27.04 will ship with the Linux 7.6 kernel, which includes better VRAM management for gaming and expanded support for modern hardware, such as early enablement for AMD Zen 6, stable support for Intel Xe3P, mainline boot capabilities for Apple M3 Pro/Max/Ultra, and initial support for the 2026 Steam Controller.

There will also be performance gains for both the Btrfs and Ext4 file systems, which (along with the improvements in GNOME 52) will make Ubuntu 27.04 one of the best-performing releases in some time.

Also: This lightweight Linux distro revives old PCs destined for the junk pile – and it’s beautiful

One thing that surprised me is that Myna (Ubuntu’s AI dictation tool) has yet to find its way into the Ubuntu ISO as a default app. As with Ubuntu 26.10, you can install it, but you have to first add the necessary repository with:

With the repository added, you can install it with:

Once installed, you can use it as expected.

As of right now, that’s all we know about Tenacious T-Rex.

It’s so early in the release cycle that it still uses the default 26.10 wallpaper, but there will be more information soon. I will say this: I’ve come to count on Ubuntu’s latest releases to be an improvement over the previous iterations, and from what I’ve seen so far in my testing, 27.04 will not disappoint. It may not knock you back to prehistoric times, but Tenacious T-Rex will wow you with its performance and polished looks.

Also: Linux has hundreds of distros: 5 reasons to stop using the same few

It’s been a very long time since Canonical had a disappointing release, and 27.04 will keep up that trend.

#3073. Why Urban Outfitters Stock Crashed on Wednesday

Anthropologie isn't turning around fast enough to please Urban Outfitters investors.

By Rich Smith – Nov 25, 2026 at 1:03PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Urban Outfitters ›

Urban Outfitters (URBN -9.39%) stock tumbled 12.1% through 12:40 p.m. ET Wednesday despite beating (barely) on Q3 earnings last night.

Heading into the report, analysts expected Urban Outfitters to earn $1.52 per share on $1.67 billion in quarterly sales. As it turned out, Urban Outfitters earned $1.54 per share, while sales met the consensus.

That hardly seems like the kind of results to spark a 12% sell-off! And yet it did. So what went wrong?

Brand by brand, growth was weakest at Anthropologie, responsible for 40% of sales -- but sales there inched up only 3.2%. The namesake Urban Outfitters brand grew its sales 4.6%. FP Group ("Free People") saw the briskest sales growth -- a whopping 14.6%, contributing most of the growth for the quarter.

Anthropologie's relatively weak performance appears to underlie today's falling share price. Commenting on the results last night, Morgan Stanley analyst Alex Straton complained that she had hoped to see recent "green shoots" at Anthropologie sprout into much bigger sales than actually materialized in Q3.

With "Anthro improvement increasingly necessary to unlock investor appreciation of the broader portfolio's value," says Straton -- and that improvement taking longer to arrive -- the worry now is that investors may have to buckle down and prepare to endure "Anthro's more prolonged deterioration."

With analysts now anticipating Urban Outfitters will grow earnings only about 5% annually over the next five years, even a relatively modest 13x price-to-earnings ratio may not be cheap enough to make Urban Outfitters stock a buy.

What could that look like on a Mac? A coding assistant could inspect a private project, make a change, run the tests, and use the results to revise its fix. A document app could summarize a folder of sensitive files while keeping the processing on the device.

PrismML says Bonsai 2.5 runs on Mac, iPhone, and iPad through MLX. Its Apple silicon package is about 8.9 GB, and the model card walks through setup on a Mac. The weights are available for free under Apache 2.0.

#3070. Your Wear OS smartwatch just got a new way to save battery life

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

It could make your Pixel Watch or Samsung Galaxy Watch more power efficient.

Some of the most popular Android smartwatches just got a battery-saving update. Google released an updated version of Google Play Services on Tuesday that can help extend the battery life of a Wear OS smartwatch.

The v26.45 update concerns location tracking during outdoor workouts. Wear OS smartwatch users can now use their phone’s Global Navigation Satellite System to track their location during an outdoor workout, which can conserve battery life by outsourcing the smartwatch’s energy to the smartphone when it isn’t in Battery Saver mode.

Also: Pixel Watch 4 vs. Watch 5: Is Google’s new model worth it?

Constantly communicating with satellites during an outdoor workout can be a battery drain, and every minute of battery life counts when you use your smartwatch for communication, workout tracking, and health monitoring. GPS services, a bright, always-on display, and continuous health sensors like SpO2 can squeeze the most juice out of your smartwatch.

Wear OS software is used by many of the most popular smartwatch brands, including Google, Samsung, and OnePlus. Both the Google Pixel Watch and Samsung Galaxy Watch’s largest batteries last approximately 40 hours. That’s nearly two days of use from two top Android smartwatches, but you’d be surprised how quickly it can drain.

Also: Galaxy Watch 9 review: Health data overload, but built for the future

The update improves battery life without users having to take any action or change any settings — the Google Play Services version 26.45 works quietly under the hood.

That’s not the only Google Play Services update that Wear OS smartwatch users can take advantage of. Another recent update lets users view on their phone a larger preview of any watch face they want to install on their smartwatch.

#3069. Can an App Tell When Someone Near You Is Wearing Smart Glasses?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Apps such as Zuckoff scan for the Bluetooth signals smart glasses send out, giving bystanders a way to know a pair is nearby.

Meta’s smart glasses stay connected to the wearer’s phone over Bluetooth, and that connection is what detector apps look for. Apps such as Zuckoff scan for the short broadcast signals Bluetooth devices send out and compare them with signals from known smart glasses models. When there’s a match, the app sends an alert. It’s a practical way to learn that a pair is nearby, though the alert can’t confirm whether anyone’s recording, and glasses with Bluetooth switched off won’t appear at all. Here’s how the apps work and how much weight to give an alert.

It’s a clever workaround for glasses designed to blend in. How useful it is depends on what you want it to tell you: The app can detect that a pair is close by, but not whether it’s recording. Still, that’s more notice than most people get today, especially if they haven’t spotted the glasses’ built-in LED indicator.

Here’s how those apps work, what they reliably catch and what they miss.

Zuckoff, whose name takes a direct jab at Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, has joined a small ecosystem of apps such as Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner and Nearby Glasses that offer similar functionality — letting you know when someone has smart glasses activated and how close the device is, although they can’t tell you specifically whether someone is actively recording or using AI to pull up information. The apps detect approximate device proximity by sweeping local Bluetooth frequencies to locate vendor IDs, system identifiers and hardware signatures associated with smart glasses.

As Zuckoff’s website notes: “Glasses advertise loudest while powering on, pairing or leaving the case. Once paired to their owner’s phone, they can go quiet, so silence is not proof that nobody is recording, and a detection is not proof that anyone is. Signal strength gives a rough distance and no direction at all.”

Zuckoff’s developer, Pawel Szydlowski, said he was already working on projects that used Bluetooth to detect nearby devices and discovered the tech could be applied to smart glasses. “It’s just the same technology wrapped in a different paper,” he said in a video chat with CNET.

Recent reports have shown that smart glasses are being used for everything from bullying in schools to viral videos with unwitting subjects who don’t know they’re being recorded.

Since it launched in early August, the Zuckoff app has gotten 2,000 sign-ups, and Szydlowski is beta-testing an Android version he hopes to make available on the Google Play Store. The app also has a premium version for $10 a year that can run continuous detection checks in the background when the app isn’t in use.

But a booming ecosystem of DIY modifications and third-party hardware hacks is also giving smart glasses wearers unprecedented stealth by allowing them to disable the activation lights, either by bypassing the capture LEDs or by patching software to suppress system notifications.

Tech journalist Joanna Stern hosted a video showing the process in which a local hacker removed the LED light from her Ray-Ban Meta glasses for $100, allowing the wearables to secretly record without notice.

Detecting active smart glasses in public or private spaces adds a new layer of security awareness, but it raises an obvious dilemma: What do you actually do with that information? Once a detector app alerts us that smart glasses are nearby, it seems our only choices are to either leave the space or ask the wearer to remove the glasses.

Uttara Ananthakrishnan, an associate professor of information systems at the University of Washington who studies the societal impacts of technology, says we’re still figuring out the social norms around wearables like smart glasses. It’s impossible to know whether the person filming will behave responsibly, and the question of consent gets even thornier if children might be captured on video or in photos.

“Until we develop clear mechanisms to balance seamless innovation with consent, these devices will continue to turn everyday public spaces into zones of surveillance anxiety,” she said.

The Even G2 smart glasses don’t have a camera for recording photos or videos. They can pair with a separately sold R1 control ring that works as a fitness tracker.

For instance, Even Realities’ G2 smart glasses don’t include a front-facing camera at all. Instead, the Even G2 devices, released in late 2025, focus on providing the wearer with information and acting more like a personal assistant.

“We made the decision from the beginning that smart glasses don’t need to have cameras on them in order to be useful,” Even Realities CEO Will Wang told CNET in an email. “We believe something worn on your face should respect not only the person wearing it, but everyone around them.”

The G2 devices don’t record externally, a design choice Wang said gave the company a unique challenge. “Leaving the camera out also pushed us to think differently about what actually makes smart glasses useful day to day, rather than assuming more sensors automatically make a better product,” he said.

Wang said there’s room in the smart glasses market for different approaches to features and functionality, and that buyers may want to make trade-offs for devices they’ll wear on their faces. But Wang noted that the rise of smart glasses detectors indicates that social acceptance is an issue the industry needs to consider.

Over the last several months, smart glasses have been getting cheaper. And with more models and companies jumping into the fray, the demand for surveillance detectors is likely to grow — that is, unless Big Tech and wearable companies radically change their devices to make them invisible to detector apps.

Szydlowski said his hope is that, in time, Zuckoff won’t be needed at all. He pointed out that the ability to detect nearby Apple AirTag devices eventually became part of the operating systems on iOS and Android devices. If consumers pressure manufacturers and their governments to make smart glasses easier to detect, it would be “the perfect solution” to make his app obsolete, he said.

#3068. An annoying ‘mistake’ in macOS was actually prep for the latest MacBook Pro

You may remember that Apple made a seeming mistake in the user interface for macOS 26, meaning that attempts to resize windows would often fail. The reason for this has now become clear, and Apple has done something both fun and clever in macOS 27 to resolve it …

I was one of a number of people to note that trying to grab the corner of a window in macOS Tahoe in order to resize it would often fail. Developer Norbert Heger pointed out this is because Apple changed the radius of the corners without changing the grabbable area.

It turns out that my initial click in the window corner instinctively happens in an area where the window doesn’t respond to it. The window expects this click to happen in an area of 19 × 19 pixels, located near the window corner. If the window had no rounded corners at all, 62% of that area would lie inside the window. But due to the huge corner radius in Tahoe, most of it – about 75% – now lies outside the window.

At the time, the radius change itself looked like an inexplicable mistake on Apple’s part, and the company did revert it. However, Macworld’s Michael Simon appears to have discovered the reason for the original change.

The new rounder corners on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR are basically a perfect match for the macOS 26 radii.

So if you move a window to the corner of the new machine, it would fit perfectly. However, since Apple reverted the corner radius, it would no longer do so. The company solved this by a clever UI transition.

What’s happening there is Golden Gate’s 20-point corner radius is subtly and gradually expanding when It approaches the bottom corner of the screen to match the exact corner of the display, which is much larger. I can’t be certain it’s exactly 26-point, but it sure looks like it to me. The effect is incredible. I’ve watched it like 20 times and I can barely see it changing, yet when it reaches the corner it’s perfectly expanded to match.

You can see this illustrated by a GIF in the Macworld piece. While the original change annoyed me, Apple’s solution is the perfect example of the company sweating the details.

This adds up to the bullish market reaction you'd expect after a robust financial report.

Both cousins are wrestling with the same industrywide memory shortage, which pushed DRAM and storage up to roughly 40% of HP Inc.'s PC component costs last quarter. In fact, the personal systems division's operating margin took a beating, dipping to a razor-thin 3% as consumer demand cooled.

#3065. Microsoft declares a Code Red in response to worst ever outage

The recent Microsoft 365 outage was the worst the service had ever experienced, with more than 80% of the company’s servers unresponsive at the worst point. The company has now declared a Code Red to address the way it prevents and responds to major failures in future.

Microsoft has explained more about why it took so long to resolve the issue and said that it’s urgently working on new approaches to resolve any future incidents in less than an hour …

Code Red is a common term used to describe the highest priority response to a major problem, pulling a significant number of engineers off their current tasks in order to maximize the resources applied to fixing it.

The senior execs responsible for the service told staff that it was the most customer-impacting incident ever experienced, and has acknowledged that not only was the problem itself unacceptable, but so too was the time taken to resolve it. Reuters got sight of a memo sent to the team.

It was the most ⁠customer-impacting incident in the history of Exchange Online, M365 Core President Jason Henderson said in a memo to staff on Friday. Never before had so many customers been without email for so long, he said. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson added.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, told a Code Red review that the affected component had experienced “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures,” according to Silver’s memo.

One reason it took so long to work out what had happened was because the diagnostic data needed was “scattered across fragmented internal systems.” The memo says 11 separate Teams chats exchanged more than 11,000 messages as they struggled to work out what exactly had gone wrong.

Microsoft is now working on five interrelated approaches to achieve a target resolution time of less than an hour for any future incidents of this nature.

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

While most AI-powered peripherals record only phone calls or in-person chats, the Ear Note is designed to capture every conversation.

Phone-maker Nothing Technology is breaking away from its typical retro-inspired designs with a new pair of AI-powered earbuds, as reported earlier by Bloomberg. The company confirmed via an X post that its Ear Note wireless earbuds will be available starting Dec. 8.

The Ear Note earbuds are designed primarily to maximize the recording functionality. While other AI earbuds have already hit the market, the Ear Note is the first to record both phone calls and in-person conversations.

Nothing shared that the Ear Note will work with multiple popular AI agents, but the full list of compatible software has not yet been released. The Ear Note works in tandem with an app that stores recordings from the earbuds and case, creating transcriptions and summaries similar to those created by the popular Otter AI app.

The Nothing brand has developed a cult following for combining lifestyle and fashion trends in its suite of smartphones, headphones, speakers and watches.

The full product lineup is built with modern hardware, but mimics warm, nearly retrofuturist design sensibilities. The blocky Ear Note charging case continues this trend while taking the company’s tech in a new direction.

In the lead-up to the Ear Note’s reveal, Nothing CEO Carl Pei described the earbuds in an X post as “a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product.”

In a Bloomberg interview, Pei indicated that Nothing isn’t trying to create AI agents or software, but that the company has a “really interesting opportunity to be the hardware layer to AI.”

It’s currently unclear how much the Ear Note earbuds and case will cost when they’re released next month. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the company hasn’t settled on a price just yet. The most expensive earbuds currently available on the Nothing store cost $149.

Whether you’re covering your eyes, plugging your ears or slapping a timepiece on your wrist, there’s now an ever-present option to record the world around you. Multiple companies have created their own versions of smart glasses, earbuds and watches with augmented reality capabilities.

Now that AI is the flavor du jour, these existing features are being enhanced by new ways to scan and interact with the surrounding environment. That means a lot of visual and auditory data is being recorded by wearable devices, and very rarely with the consent of all parties involved.

The most immediate risk factors are associated with video recording – public distrust of smart glasses is so widespread that they’ve colloquially been coined “pervert glasses,” as folks fear they fundamentally break an unspoken social contract by obscuring public recording from other people.

But audio recording, enabled by Apple’s latest smartwatches, the Amazon Bee, Plaud earbuds and the new Ear Note, is also raising concerns, not least because many states require all-party consent before you can record conversations.

The Ear Note’s ability to record every bit of audio, from phone calls to in-person conversations, means it will be handling more sensitive information than other AI-powered earbuds. The company will need to face new challenges to ensure security measures are in place to prevent private chats from leaking.

Pei called wearables with recording functionality a sensitive space, and said the design team was “extra careful to not take any risks.” The Ear Note earbuds and case are largely controlled by user commands, including tactile button presses that begin the recording process.

The program could create a personalized feed like “John’s Channel,” stocked with AI-made crime-comedy capers, rom-coms and sci-fi adventures, if those are the shows John enjoys. The service could make new videos based on voice prompts or create new ones on its own, the report said.

Building a channel of AI slop isn’t a new idea. Roku recently unveiled FairgroundTV, the first free, all-AI streaming channel.

Generative AI continues to draw widespread skepticism from both local communities and everyday internet users. New data centers built to power AI models have met growing grassroots resistance over their heavy energy and water footprints, while synthetic content faces mounting cultural pushback, especially from younger audiences, who have largely rejected AI-generated media as inauthentic “slop.”

#3061. WhatsApp testing stickers with audio, including make-your-own option

WhatsApp is currently testing a new sticker format that plays a sound when the recipient taps on it. You can choose from a range of standard stickers as well as create your own by converting a video …

The feature was spotted by WABetaInfo in the beta version of the Android app.

WhatsApp is developing a new format to add an audio track to a sticker. This would allow users to send a sticker that plays a sound when the recipient taps it.

You can create your own audio stickers by selecting one of your videos.

Once users choose a video from their gallery, WhatsApp converts it into an animated sticker automatically. At the top of the editor, users can find a new audio button that lets them add a sound to the sticker. If users tap this button, WhatsApp will display a new “Add sound” screen. This section lets users refine the new sound sticker by choosing which audio track to attach to it.

Sounds don’t play automatically, but recipients will see a small audio icon attached to the sticker, and tapping it will play the sound.

As usual with WhatsApp, it’s rolling out first in the Android beta and is likely to reach the iPhone sometime later. This can range from a few weeks to a few months, depending on how well the beta test goes.

#3060. 5 new Apple Health features you should try in iOS 27.3 – if your phone qualifies

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Apple's redesigned Health app arrives in December with some major upgrades, but not every iPhone will get the full experience.

Apple is kicking off a new and improved Health app next month with the release of iOS 27.3. Instead of just recording and displaying your health-related stats, the app will tap into Apple Intelligence to analyze the data and dispense advice on how to improve your health and fitness. But that reliance on AI means you’ll need the right type of iPhone to enjoy all the benefits.

Also: Apple could build its AI health chatbot from this study – how to enroll

Here are five helpful new features built into the app, along with what you’ll need to access them.

First up, the app will offer suggestions based on data from different sources. For example, it might advise you to go for a walk at a nearby park if it detects that you’re not getting enough exercise. It may show you articles and videos about sleep if it finds that you’re not well-rested. It could also highlight possible conditions based on your lab and test results. You can easily view these recommendations from the Insights screen.

Also: Health is Tim Cook’s defining legacy – and your Apple Watch proves it

A new feature called Health Age compares your physical health to your actual age to show how you’re doing. The analysis draws on certain stats and lab data, such as your resting heart rate, sleep, heart rate variability (HRV), cholesterol, and A1C (average blood glucose levels), to deliver a health age, which may differ from your chronological age. The results can show you areas that may be of concern or that you need to focus on.

Also: Apple Watch Series 12 review: Finally, the health tracker I’ve been waiting for

With a new feature called Movement Evaluations and an iPhone and Apple Watch, the Health app can assess your flexibility, strength, balance, VO2 max (maximum oxygen absorption), and overall movement. You perform a physical routine while your iPhone “watches” you via the camera. Using built-in AI, the app will provide audio and visual feedback in real-time to tell you how you’re faring.

Apple promises that the analysis is performed on your device without recording, storing, or sharing the video.

The new app will be able to correlate your test results with data collected by your iPhone and Apple Watch to give you a more comprehensive picture of your health. Plus, Apple and Quest Diagnostics have teamed up to offer people in the US an optional $119 bloodwork panel that covers more than 50 biomarkers to scan for different health and medical conditions.

Also: I tested the Apple Watch Series 12 heart-rate claims against my gold-standard Polar strap

Normally, you need an Apple Fitness+ subscription to fire up workout videos to help you exercise. But the new Health app will come with its own comprehensive set of training videos. Available from the Insights section, a series of strength exercise videos are designed to help you build your body strength. The videos cover all the key areas of your body to give you a full workout.

Some of the new features, such as the strength videos, will be available to all iPhone users. But the ones that rely on AI will run only on phones that support Apple Intelligence. That means you’ll need an iPhone 15 Pro or Pro Max, any iPhone 16 or 17, an iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max, an iPhone Air, or an iPhone Duo.
