#2997. Super Hi (HDL) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Southeast and East Asia held up as North America lagged on sales.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 25, 2026 at 1:37PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Super Hi (HDL +6.93%) reported a 7.1% year-over-year revenue increase for the third quarter, driven by higher guest traffic and an expanded restaurant network despite same-store sales pressure in North America. The company reported a significant increase in net profit due to nonoperating foreign exchange gains, while operating margins were impacted by phased investments in secondary brands and the centralization of management support functions. Management reported that Southeast Asia and East Asia remained resilient, whereas the North American market requires strategic adjustments to menu pricing and guest engagement to reach mainstream local diners. The company continues to advance its multi-brand strategy through the Pomegranate Plan and is leveraging digital tools to refine its loyalty program, which currently contributes 90% of restaurant revenue.

Operator: Hello, investors and analysts. Thank you so much for joining Super Hi International's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. With us today are Mr. Yu Li, Executive Director and CEO; and Ms. Lu Li, Chief Financial Officer and Joint Company Secretary. Today's call may contain forward-looking statements, including statements about our strategy, business plans and outlook. The information we present today and our comments and answers to your questions reflect management's views as of today. Please refer to the latest safe harbor statement in our earnings release, which also applies to this call. The call will be conducted in Mandarin with simultaneous English interpretation provided by an external provider. In the event of any discrepancy, the Chinese remarks will prevail.

Today's slides are available on our Investor Relations website. Now I'll turn the call over to Mr. Yu Li, our CEO and Executive Director, to review our third quarter 2026 results.

Yu Li: Thank you. Hello, investors and analysts. I'm Yu Li, CEO and Executive Director of Super Hi International. Let me walk you through our operating performance for the third quarter of 2026. This quarter, we stayed with our long-term strategy of focusing on both employees and guests. We worked to improve the guest experience, refine our menu and manage each restaurant more closely. Haidilao restaurants served 8.4 million guest visits, up 3.7% year-over-year. Both overall and same-store average table turnover reached 4x per day, up 0.1 turn each. Haidilao restaurant revenue rose by 2.4%. We also continue to grow revenue beyond dine-in and advance our Pomegranate Plan. Combined revenue from delivery and other businesses grew by 78.2% year-over-year.

That helped lift total revenue to $229 million, up 7.1% year-over-year and 4.8% quarter-over-quarter. Operating profit was $9.933 million with an operating margin of 4.3%. As we improved operations at existing restaurants, we also continued to expand our network. We opened 3 Haidilao restaurants and began putting resources in place for upcoming openings. We continue to explore additional brands and strengthen our shared support functions at headquarters. Related investment at this stage was higher than a year ago. Operating profit improved from the second quarter, but remained below the prior-year level. Let me walk you through our main initiatives this quarter. First, we stayed focused on restaurant operations and adapted guest engagement and staff management to each market.

We continue to give regions and restaurants flexibility. Local teams could adjust how they operated based on local spending conditions, their guest mix and each restaurant's performance. We also stepped up frontline training, staffing and day-to-day management. As preparations for new openings progressed, we began recruiting and training for key roles in advance. To date, more than 60% of our restaurants have trained managers ready to step up. That gives us a talent pipeline for new openings and ongoing operations. In guest engagement, we put more weight on how much a campaign actually drives traffic and repeat visits alongside discounts it offers.

Take Vietnam, our restaurants improved loyalty benefits, engaged staff to bring in new guests and maintained closer ties with guest communities. They also ran campaigns around local holidays and dining occasions. These efforts helped attract new guests and bring loyalty members back. Second, we continue to make Haidilao distinctive in each market. We stepped up local menu development and refined our menus, building on ingredients and dishes familiar to local guests. We tracked whether new dishes could sustain sales and generate repeat orders after launch. In Singapore, we introduced laksa hot pot and tender pork belly rolls, bringing familiar local flavors to hot pot.

In Korea, we focused on beef, specialty broths and snacks, launching thick-cut beef oyster blade, a rich chestnut and chicken broth and mini milk buns. In Vietnam, we introduced specialty beef and mushroom and vegetable platters to add more choices for local celebrations and group meals. Japan, Canada and Australia also kept adjusting their menus based on seasonal demand, ingredient quality and local taste. We track what guests order, which dishes they order again and how much revenue those dishes contribute. We use that data along with local supply conditions to adjust the menu mix. Our aim is to offer guests more choice while managing menus and running food operations more efficiently.

Third, we continue to strengthen our shared support functions at headquarters. We built on our routine performance tracking by looking at more data together that included table turnover, operating data, member behavior, menu mix, marketing campaigns, costs and expenses. This helps regional teams pinpoint issues and take actions. On the menu side, we use dish click-through rate, repeat orders, sales contribution and gross margin to guide menu changes and new item launches. In marketing, we review the returns on set menus and campaigns and assess their impact on traffic, sales and profit. Restaurants can then adjust pricing and promotions more quickly. At the end of September, Haidilao had more than 10 million registered loyalty members overseas.

As the membership grows, we are focusing on keeping members active and turning that engagement into repeat spending. We look at how often different groups dine with us and how long they go between visits, so restaurants can tailor their outreach. We also share lessons across markets and translate our analysis into practical steps for restaurants. This helps headquarters provide more effective support to frontline teams. Fourth, we continue to expand the Haidilao network at a measured pace with close attention to how new restaurants operate. We opened 3 Haidilao restaurants this quarter, bringing the overseas total to 132 at the end of September. One more has already opened in the fourth quarter and 6 others are preparing to open.

Based on our current progress, we expect 13 openings for the full year. Local teams continue to identify opportunities based on market demand, changes in trade areas, the talent pipeline and projected investment returns. Headquarters supports them by visiting proposed sites, assessing management candidates, reviewing project risks and testing the assumptions behind projections. This helps us pace our openings. Fifth, we continue to advance the Pomegranate Plan and test different restaurant formats across markets. At quarter end of this quarter, we operated 26 restaurants overseas under other brands. They included Malatang, Barbecue, Izakaya and Halal Hot Pot. Several concepts have begun to establish their operating models and show early signs of profitability.

At Hi Bowl, our Malatang concept, we've developed a quick-service model with relatively high seat turnover and relatively low upfront investment. Our Canadian location has been profitable at the restaurant level for several consecutive months, and our Japanese location was profitable at the restaurant level throughout the quarter. Our Izakaya in Japan has also been profitable at the restaurant level for several consecutive months after we refined the menu mix and staffing. Performance still varies considerably across these concepts. The Pomegranate Plan as a whole is still in the investment and business model validation stage. For concepts that are performing well, we'll continue to refine the menu, supply chain and management model.

Where results are below expectations, we'll keep making adjustments and carefully assess the next steps. Overall, we continued to improve existing restaurant operations this quarter while expanding our network and diversifying our business. As conditions evolve across markets, we'll keep our focus on both employees and guests. We'll strengthen the support headquarters provides, improve operations at each restaurant and keep the company on a steady path for long-term growth. Thank you. That concludes my review of third quarter operations. I'll now turn the call over to Lu Li to discuss our financial results.

Lu Li: Thank you, Yu. Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining the call. I am Lu Li, the company's CFO. I'll walk you through Super Hi International's financial and operating results for the third quarter of 2026. Total revenue was $229 million, up 7.1% from $214 million a year ago and up 4.8% from the second quarter. Haidilao restaurant revenue was $206 million, up 2.4% year-over-year. We had a net increase of 6 Haidilao restaurants from a year ago. Overall table turnover and guest visits were also higher, which supported restaurant revenue. Beyond dine-in, we continue to invest in delivery and broaden the range of items available online. Delivery revenue was approximately $7.85 million, up approximately 77.3% year-over-year.

Other revenue was approximately $15.9 million, up 78.7% year-over-year. It came mainly from sales of food products and seasonings from the Haidilao brand and our own central kitchens as well as restaurant revenue from new brands under the Pomegranate Plan. Turning to costs and expenses. Raw materials and consumables cost $79.611 million. Overall gross margin was 65.3%, down 1.4 percentage points year-over-year. Staff costs were $78.791 million or about 34.2% of revenue. That was up about 1 percentage point from 33.2% a year ago. Since the start of the year, we've continued to improve existing restaurant operations while steadily expanding Haidilao and our other brands. We began preparing new locations and putting staff in place ahead of openings.

Preopening investment was higher than a year ago. We also strengthened the shared support functions at headquarters and stepped up investment in building and training our talent pipeline. At Haidilao restaurants, margins remained stable to slightly higher year-over-year. Part of the change in group-level costs reflects our continued investment in expansion and in strengthening those shared management capabilities. Rent and related expenses were $6.483 million or about 2.8% of revenue. Utilities were $8.284 million or about 3.6% of revenue. Both ratios were broadly flat year-over-year. Depreciation and amortization came to $22.384 million or about 9.8% of revenue, down 0.2 percentage points. Travel and other operating expenses were $28.987 million or about 10.9% of revenue, down about 0.2 percentage points.

Those last 2 ratios fell mainly because revenue increased. Operating profit was approximately $9.933 million, with an operating margin of 4.3%. Operating profit fell 21.4% year-over-year, and operating margin declined 1.6 percentage points. This mainly reflected the increased investment I mentioned in business expansion and management capabilities. Compared with the second quarter, operating profit rose by about 22.2% and operating margin increased by 0.6 percentage points from 3.7% to 4.3%. Profit after tax for this quarter was $9.226 million, up 155.6% from $3.593 million a year ago. We recorded a net foreign exchange gain of $4.63 million compared with a net foreign exchange loss of $5.813 million a year earlier. That was a positive swing of approximately $10.443 million.

This year-over-year increase in net profit was, therefore, driven mainly by the improvement in nonoperating foreign exchange results. Net cash generated from operating activities was $36.18 million, up 6.2% from $38.14 million a year ago. At September 30, 2026, bank balances and cash stood at approximately $243 million. Our liquidity remains strong. Let me now turn to our key restaurant metrics. At quarter end, we operated 132 Haidilao restaurants overseas. We recorded about 8.4 million guest visits this quarter, up about 3.7% year-over-year. Average table turnover was 4x per day, up 0.1 turn. Average spending per guest was $24.5, down approximately $0.1.

That mainly reflected a shift in the guest mix with markets where guests spend less per visit accounting for a higher share of our traffic. Average daily revenue per restaurant was $17,700, down about 1.7% year-over-year. Same-store table turnover was 4x per day, up 0.1 turn. While turnover improved overall, changes in average spending per guest and traffic across regions continue to affect same-store sales. Group-wide same-store sales fell 2.3% year-over-year. Southeast Asia was broadly flat. East Asia grew, and same-store sales in North America and other regions remained under pressure. Let me now take a closer look at the figures by region. Performance varied considerably by region this quarter, with Southeast Asia and East Asia remaining broadly resilient.

We opened 2 Haidilao restaurants in Southeast Asia, 1 in Vietnam and 1 in Indonesia. Average table turnover rose from 3.7x to 4x per day year-over-year. Same-store turnover rose by 0.1 turn to 3.9x per day. Overall guest traffic improved. Average spending per guest was $18.7, down $0.4. At same stores, it was slightly higher at $19.2, down $0.1. The differences mainly reflect where the new restaurants opened. Higher table turnover helped lift average daily sales per restaurant by 0.6% to $15,600. Now in East Asia, average table turnover held at 4.9x per day. Same-store turnover was 5x per day, up 0.1 turn. Mature restaurants continue to perform well.

Average spending per guest was $28.8, both overall and at same stores, down slightly year-over-year. This mainly reflected a weaker Japanese yen against the U.S. dollar. At constant exchange rates, overall spending per guest rose $0.40. Average daily sales per restaurant were $20,300, broadly flat year-over-year. We still see room for improvement in North America and other regions. As local dining habits and market conditions evolve, guests in some markets are paying closer attention to price and the dining experience. In some markets, the guest mix and what people want are also changing. That makes it more demanding for restaurants to attract new guests and retain existing ones. We opened 1 new Haidilao restaurant in the United States this quarter.

In North America, both overall and same-store table turnover were 3.4x per day, down 0.6 and 0.5 turns respectively year-over-year. Average spending per guest was $41.5 overall and $40.8 at same stores, both were higher than a year ago. Since the start of the year, we've upgraded what's included in some of our North America set menus with slightly higher starting prices. Average daily sales per restaurant were $19,600, down about 11.3% year-over-year. Canada was the main drag on operating efficiency in the region. Our Canadian team continues to adjust pricing on individual dishes and set menus in line with local dining habits and price sensitivity. It is also offering set menus during off-peak hours to draw guests in.

In other regions, we operate 12 restaurants, all were open for more than 75 days in both the current and prior year quarters and are included in our same-store base. So the metrics are the same for both groups. Average table turnover was 3.5x per day, down 0.2 turn. Average spending per guest was $41.5, up $2.1 year-over-year. At constant exchange rates, it was up $0.20 or broadly flat. Lower turnover weighed on restaurant operating efficiency. Average daily sales per restaurant were $22,300, down about 2.6%. That concludes our review of the company's third quarter 2026 financial and operating results. Thank you. We'll now open the floor to questions from investors and analysts.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The first question comes from Zheshang Securities. [ Ms. Zhong Yichen ], please go ahead.

Unknown Analyst: My name is [ Zhong Yichen]. I actually have 2 questions. The first one is about overseas competition. More and more Chinese restaurant brands now are expanding overseas. The competition has intensified. How does competition vary by country? And what impact has it had on your table turnover and rents? How do you plan to respond as more brands go overseas? That's my first question. My second question is that, since the beginning of the year, Haidilao in China has been building shared support functions and gradually shifting some functional responsibilities away from restaurant managers. How far along are you overseas? Where do restaurant managers and regional teams still have discretion?

Yu Li: Thank you, [ Ms. Zhong ], for your questions. Let me take both of your questions. Now regarding your first question, yes, indeed, more and more Chinese restaurant brands are right now entering the overseas market in recent years. That brings more competition, but it also helps familiarize consumers overseas with Chinese food and expands the market. In some Asia Pacific markets, demand for Chinese food is already well established and competition is more about how restaurants differentiate their menus and guest experience. In Europe and North America, there is still considerable room to build brands. We compete with Chinese restaurants and also a wide range of local operators as well.

The impact on table turnover and rents varies by market. Turnover depends on consumer demands, traffic in the trade area and how well the restaurant is run, among other factors. Competition is one of those factors. When choosing new locations, we look at competition in the trade area, lease terms and also the return we need from the projects. We keep investment costs under tight control. We will keep focusing on both employees and guests. We'll develop more products for local tastes, improve our service experience and strengthen our loyalty program to reach more mainstream local diners. We believe lasting competitiveness comes down to the food, service and our ability to run individual restaurants well and consistently.

Now regarding your second question, we are moving in the same direction as Haidilao in China. We want restaurant managers to spend more time on guests, staff and day-to-day operations. Shared tools and specialist support are gradually being centralized. Headquarters already provides shared support to regional teams in areas including digital systems, operating analysis, financial management and supply chain management. Dining habits, labor laws -- I mean, rules and supply conditions vary considerably from country to country. So we'll continue to give regional teams substantial operating autonomy and flexibility. Regions and restaurants can adapt product development, pricing, marketing, customer acquisition and staff management to local conditions. We maintain common standards for food safety, service quality and compliance.

Shared support gives restaurant managers more time to focus on guests and employees while preserving frontline discretion and improving the quality and efficiency of restaurant operations. That's all for my answer.

Operator: The next question comes from Shengwei Lai with CICC.

Shengwei Lai: I am Shengwei Lai from CICC. I have 3 small questions. The first one is about North America. Well, what are your priorities for improving the North America business over the next few quarters? Which steps are most likely to make a meaningful difference in reaching mainstream local diners, driving repeat visits and improving your restaurant footprint? What do you expect to see? And when do you expect to see the results? My second question is about the restaurant growth outlook. Since the fourth quarter began, what changes have you seen in consumer demand and restaurant traffic in Southeast Asia, East Asia and North America? Looking ahead to next year, what will drive same-store growth by region?

And which markets are you most confident about? And my last question is about margin. Now we actually see that you have put in new investment this quarter. What will be the main levers for improving the group's operating margin next year? How much room is there to improve labor productivity, source locally and turn around underperforming restaurants? How will you pace investment in shared profit -- I mean, shared support functions as revenue grows?

Yu Li: All right. This is Yu Li. I'm going to take your first question. Now regarding North America, North America has been affected by changes in demand and competition locally. We also have work to do on understanding the market, managing operations and responding more quickly. We were slow to spot and act on some market changes. We've begun restructuring the management team to strengthen local operations and help our teams pick up on changes sooner and execute faster. We're working on 3 fronts. First, we are reviewing and adjusting our local operating strategy to give guests more reasons to visit.

Some restaurants have changed dishes and set menus based on market feedback, launched themed weekend events and focused more on students. We'll keep tracking what works and adjust our approach to each market and restaurant. Second, we are managing each restaurant more closely and refining the network. We'll take a closer look at traffic by location and time of the day, menu mix, staffing and operating costs. This will help us target improvements at individual restaurants. Third, we want to broaden our guest base. While retaining existing diners, we will reach out to more mainstream local guests with targeted products, campaigns and local marketing. We want to attract more new diners and gradually bring more of them back.

We hope to see early results from some marketing and operational changes over the next 1 to 2 quarters. It will take longer to assess shifts in the guest mix, where repeat visit rates settle and whether individual restaurants sustain their improvement. That's my answer for your first question. Now Ms. Lu Li is going to take the other 2 of your questions.

Lu Li: Now regarding your second question, basically, overseas markets are moving into the traditional peak dining season. Demand for holiday and year-end group meals has increased. Traffic has improved overall, and table turnover is higher year-over-year. Some markets in East and Southeast Asia stood out, and East Asia as a whole held steady. Some North American restaurants remain under pressure. We're also seeing encouraging signs in demand for business gatherings and company dinners. Our overseas restaurants are preparing to accommodate these groups and capture peak season demand. Looking ahead to 2027, we're confident that Southeast Asia and East Asia can maintain steady operations.

Same-store growth will continue to come mainly from locally developed products, the loyalty program, repeat visits and closer management at the restaurant level. In North America, we'll focus on improving existing restaurants, reaching more mainstream local diners, refining our menu and pricing and getting more guests to act on our campaigns. Overall, our priority remains running each restaurant well. We'll make the most of the peak season and keep improving the guest experience and operating efficiency to support future same-store growth. Now regarding your last question, which is about our operating efficiency. There's room to improve profitability at existing restaurants. We make decisions with operating quality in mind and balance near-term performance with long-term development.

At existing restaurants, we'll improve staffing and scheduling, strengthen procurement and source more locally. For restaurants that are falling short of expectations, we'll make targeted improvements or adjust the network. The aim is to improve efficiency and profitability at individual restaurants. Across the group, preparations for new Haidilao restaurants, new concepts under the Pomegranate Plan and shared support capabilities at headquarters all require upfront resources and investment that can affect group margins in the short term. We'll pace investment according to how the businesses evolve and what stage they're at and keep reviewing the returns on that spending. Overall, we're confident that we can keep improving profitability at existing restaurants.

We will continue making the long-term investments we need and balance them with near-term operating performance to support steady, sustainable growth. Thank you.

Operator: The next question comes from Huatai Securities. Jun Zeng, please go ahead.

Jun Zeng: I also have 3 small questions. The first one is, how did average spending per guest change year-over-year by region at constant exchange rates? How is price sensitivity changing across markets? Have you added low-price set menus or smaller portions? And how has that affected spending per guest and table turnover? With exchange rates still volatile, how do you quantify the point at which the trade-off between spending per guest and table turnover makes sense? The second question is about new restaurant openings. Now operations and profitability in East and Southeast Asia have been fairly stable across the market following recent adjustments. Are you considering taking what has worked in Asia into new markets?

How do you weigh adding more restaurants in existing countries against expanding into new regions? My third question is about delivery. Delivery revenue is growing quickly. Can every restaurant offer delivery? Are you targeting a share of revenue from delivery that protects the dine-in experience? How does average spending on delivery compare with dine-in? And what are the respective gross margins?

Yu Li: Thank you, Mr. Zeng, for your questions. First of all, regarding your first question, in the third quarter, at constant exchange rates, average spending per guest in Southeast Asia fell about $0.50 year-over-year. That mainly reflected where we opened our new restaurants. Most of this year's openings in the region were in Indonesia and Vietnam, where spending per guest is relatively lower. In East Asia, spending per guest rose by $0.40 at constant exchange rates. In North America, it rose by $2.6 year-over-year, mainly because we've refined, upgraded and introduced menu items since the first half of the year and adjusted some set menus.

In other regions, spending per guest rose by $0.20 at constant exchange rates, reflecting a small impact from menu changes. We believe that price sensitivity varies across markets, so pricing needs to vary too. In North America, the third quarter numbers show a clear impact on table turnover from changes in spending per guest. Market conditions and guest needs can change very quickly. We also realize that regional managers need to be closely involved in local operations so they can improve the experience while offering good value. When we weigh spending per guest against table turnover, we look at each restaurant's overall performance.

Headquarters look at table turnover alongside the menu mix, returns on marketing spend and gross margins to help restaurants adjust pricing and promotions. So that was my answer for your first question. Regarding your second question, yes, we have operated in Southeast and East Asia for years and have built up considerable experience adapting to local markets. Third quarter average table turnover in Southeast Asia rose from 3.7x to 4x per day year-over-year. East Asia held at 4.9x. Overall operating metrics remain fairly resilient in both regions. What travels across markets is our expertise in site selection, talent development, supply chain management, menu development and restaurant operations.

But the menu mix, pricing and marketing still need to reflect local demand in each country. We'll look at both adding restaurants in existing markets and entering new areas where we already have brand awareness, a supply chain and trained staff, and a denser network can improve operating efficiency. We'll also weigh coverage across trade areas, traffic at existing locations and whether a new restaurant could draw traffic away from them. For new regions and countries, we'll take a closer look at demand, spending power, competition, supply conditions and the availability of management talent. We've done some initial work in markets and some markets in Europe and South America, but it's still early, and there's a lot to do.

Site visits and deeper research will help us understand local conditions and prepare before we move ahead gradually. Our approach is still to identify opportunities from the ground up, with restaurant-level operating quality and long-term investment returns determining the pace of opening new stores. So that was my answer for your second question. The last question was about delivery. Now delivery has been one of our fastest-growing businesses over the past few quarters. In the third quarter of 2026, delivery revenue reached approximately $7.85 million, up 77.3% year-over-year and representing about 3.4% of group revenue. Delivery growth has come mainly from new products, marketing, broader distinction -- sorry, broader distribution and closer partnerships with local delivery platforms.

Delivery serves different occasions and operates very differently from dine-in. The delivery menu mainly offers simple meals and single-person sets. On average, a meal for one costs less on delivery than when dining in, and gross margin is also slightly lower. Delivery has lower labor costs, but it also incurs extra costs such as platform commissions. That results in different cost and profit structures. Haidilao's core strengths are food, service and the in-restaurant experience. We'll protect the experience as we grow our delivery business. At each location, we consider kitchen capacity, staffing, how busy dine-in is and local delivery demand before deciding what to offer on which platform and how. Almost all Haidilao restaurants now offer delivery services.

We look at whether delivery generates incremental revenue and profit and makes a meaningful contribution. We don't set a fixed target for its share of revenue. That's all. Thank you.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The next question comes from [ Wei Jiabao ] with CITIC Securities.

Unknown Analyst: I am [ Wei Jiabao ] with CITIC Securities. I have 2 questions. The first one is about Hi Bowl and other brands. Now Hi Bowl has expanded into markets including Singapore and Australia, and Haidilao's Dai Pai Dong concept is planned for Vietnam. Could you update us on the Pomegranate Plan, including priority brands, opening targets, markets for expansion and operating models at representative locations? And my second question is about your plan for dividends and share buybacks.

Lu Li: Thank you for the questions. Now regarding the Pomegranate Plan, the plan builds on years of experience in overseas restaurant operations, supply chains and talent management. The aim of it is to develop more dining formats suited to local consumers. To date, we have more than 10 brands and more than 30 Pomegranate Plan restaurants overseas. As Mr. Yu Li mentioned earlier, Hi Bowl, our Malatang concept, is among the concepts with a relatively clear and proven operating model. We have locations open in Canada, Japan, Australia and Singapore and projects in preparation in other countries, including the United States and United Kingdom.

Now we also see strong operating and expansion potential in hot pot, our Halal Hot Pot brand in Indonesia and our Izakaya in Japan. We've also brought in Xiangxiang Hunan Cuisine and are exploring a new model through a joint venture with an established Chinese restaurant brand. In October, we opened 1 restaurant each in South Korea, Vietnam and Indonesia. By combining the partners' strengths, we hope to use Super Hi's existing overseas platform to make it easier for new brands to enter overseas markets. Now on the Haidilao Dai Pai Dong concept you mentioned, we are preparing the first location in Vietnam and expect it to open by year-end.

At the current stage, we will first validate the restaurant-level economics of each format before deciding which concept can expand rapidly. We look at guest acceptance, revenue mix, gross profit -- I mean gross margin, labor productivity and investment returns. Where concepts perform well, we will continue to build the capabilities they need. Where results fall short, we'll make timely adjustments. Now regarding the second question of yours about dividends and share buybacks. We generated approximately $36.18 million in net cash from operating activities in the third quarter. At the end of September, bank balances and cash were approximately $243 million. Overall, liquidity remains strong.

In allocating capital, we will consider the funding needs of existing operations and planned investment in new Haidilao restaurants. We will carefully evaluate dividends and share repurchases in light of cash flow, CapEx plans, our overall financial position and shareholders' interests and follow the Board's decision-making procedures. Thank you.

Operator: Now the next question comes from [ Li Zhenni ] with Founder Securities.

Unknown Analyst: I have 2 questions here. The first question is, how are this year's new restaurants doing in terms of operating performance and margins? What investment payback periods are you seeing? My second question is, how many overseas loyalty members do you have? What shares of revenue do they account for? How are member acquisition, repeat visits and engagement trending? What are you doing differently with member behavior data and digital tools? These are my 2 questions.

Yu Li: Thank you, [ Ms. Li ], for your questions. Now about new store performance. Over the past few years, we've strengthened our upfront investment reviews and preopening preparations. That includes refining site selection criteria, restaurant design and staffing pipeline requirements. New restaurants are ramping up faster overall. By the end of September 2026, 6 new restaurants had opened, 5 generated positive cash flow in their first month, and those restaurants averaged more than 4 table turns per day in October. We continue to assess new projects against payback requirements of roughly 3 to 5 years, depending on the region. Most new restaurants currently have expected payback periods within plan.

We'll continue improving how we evaluate and prepare new restaurants and raise operating efficiency and restaurant-level profitability to support steady network growth. Now your second question is about our overseas loyalty members. Our loyalty program is an important part of strengthening how we engage with guests. At the end of September 2026, Haidilao had more than 10 million registered members overseas. Member spending accounted for approximately 90% of Haidilao restaurant revenue. As the program grows, we are refining the benefits at each membership tier. To keep members active, we offer exclusive discounts on dishes, run campaigns to bring back inactive members and provide birthday and tier rewards.

We've also launched the Haidilao App in several overseas markets, added more rewards to the points store and introduced tiered point redemption. These steps improve member experience and encourage repeat visits and stronger loyalty. On the digital side, we are deepening our analysis of member spending habits, including visit frequency, time between visits and menu preferences. We combine member, menu and operating data so restaurants can make better decisions on campaigns, guest retention and menu promotions to improve operating performance. That's my answer for your 2 questions. Thank you.

Operator: All right. Thank you for the questions. Now this concludes our earnings call. Thank you, investors and analysts, for your participation. I'll see you next time. [Statements in English on this transcript were spoken by an interpreter present on the live call.]

#2996. I Tried Using Meta Muse and ChatGPT Dots to Save on Groceries. They’re Not Quite There Yet

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

I tried using AI agents to build me the cheapest grocery order possible. They exhibited a startling lack of curiosity and autonomous thinking.

High grocery prices have been in the news for years now. The cost of eggs, how much you’re paying for a bowl of cereal and whether or not meat is back on the menu are the recurring subjects of nationwide headlines.

So before you drop a fortune on gas and drive out to the grocery store to spend even more on sustenance in your prep for hosting or bringing dishes to your holiday celebrations, you might consider using an AI agent to find you the best deal possible.

Although, in my experience, it’s not as simple as the AI marketing makes it sound. Here’s what happened when I tried to use AI agents to find the lowest possible prices on groceries.

AI agents such as Meta Muse and ChatGPT’s Dots can only crawl so many sites and online fliers for prices. Some stores and e-commerce sites have blocked AI agents from accessing their URLs. The first step in finding cheaper groceries with AI agents is to check which sites and stores they can access for price comparisons.

Where both agents missed a step was in the limitations they put on their searches, at first only looking at the retailers I had shown via my receipts and a few other big-name grocery stores.

I clarified in the chats and in a 20-minute voice conversation with Muse and a 14-minute voice conversation with Dots that they should expand their horizons and look at discount online retailers like Martie.com, and check what they could around advertised pricing and offerings at local farmers’ markets.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Muse stuck to the basics like Ralphs, Target and Walmart, and then expanded to Sprouts, Vons and Martie.com when prompted.

After further nudging, Muse also reviewed user-reported pricing from Costco (I don’t have a membership), gave me vague information about Grocery Outlet, suggested Misfits Market/Imperfect Foods, ruled out Amazon Fresh and gave me some sample pricing from a local butcher for meats.

Muse also checked some local bakery prices after I mentioned I’d like to find alternatives to sweet treats at a more affordable price.

Dots checked all the usual places that Meta Muse checked with a few extras thrown in — Smart & Final for produce, meat and some packaged products, and Super King’s monthly ad.

Neither of the tools checked Trader Joe’s. Muse said that the grocery chain doesn’t show prices of its products online, despite me finding that the Trader Joe’s website shows prices of its products online. Both Dots and Muse admitted to only checking the local store’s pages when asked.

You could spend some time making a list from scratch of all the groceries you might need every two weeks and give that list to the AI agent for its search. You could also skip all that and take some pics of your most recent grocery receipts and online payments and have the AI agent build the list itself.

I had some receipts saved, and the AI agents I used for this test were able to put together an accurate grocery list from them. I also provided emails showing receipts from online orders of household items and groceries for the past month to build my orders.

Muse took my receipts and concluded that, surprise, surprise, shopping at Gelson’s was not as cost-effective as shopping at Walmart. It spat out a lot of specific information about comparisons on some of the items in my list, but completely ignored others.

Dots looked over my receipts and recommended I try shopping at Super King for most fresh meat, produce and a few grains, and keep Walmart as my main option for packaged products like pasta sauce.

Both tools tackled this task in a way I was not expecting — as a narrative exploration of my overall grocery spending, with generalized suggestions supported by specific examples of spot pricing.

It was kind of like they’ve been optimized to write essays about grocery shopping as a school assignment, and not to be agentic personal assistants for real-world work.

Maybe it was the way I phrased the task, but I was hoping to get an actual shopping list with price comparisons for each item, or at least equivalent items, and a guide on where and how to procure said items.

Neither AI agent provided this autonomously and had to be directly prompted to provide grocery lists in response to a very specific request.

AI agents are supposed to be pros at anticipating the needs of their human bosses. I was keen to see how the always-on AI agents would handle managing the recurring needs of a small household and if they might make any autonomous suggestions meant to save me money in ways I hadn’t anticipated.

At no point did Muse seem to be actually thinking outside the strict parameters of the review of the items on the receipts I sent. This felt more like a conversation about what I’d previously purchased with a side serving of attempts to get me to connect Instacart to the tool.

It was also the most confusing grocery shopping experience I have ever had. That might be on me, but I would assume the agent might ask some questions, like how often I usually shop, what my monthly budget for groceries is, and how many people and animals live in the house. Muse didn’t ask any of those things and had to be prompted consistently.

Muse sent me the final grocery list as a raw Markdown file, which was hilarious. I got a .pdf version after explicitly asking for one.

My original total with one in-person shop and one online order was about $180. Muse’s total with three in-person shops and one online order came in at around $153.

Dots was slightly better suited to this task after some prodding, and gave me some options for building prep meals with low-effort, high-protein recipes based on how I usually shop.

Dots’ final grocery list included everything I asked for, but still missed some key items, like solid substitutes for pricey prepped foods. Dot’s final total with two in-person shopping trips and a whole lot of missing items came out to around $85.

This test reinforced my findings about how agentic AI tools tackle domestic or traditionally invisible labor tasks. In my limited use cases so far, they are about as useful as a loose dog turd tumbling around in a clothes dryer.

If you’re not looking to book a flight and hotel for a business conference in Philadelphia or put your Sweetgreen order on autopilot, the AI agents exhibit a startling lack of curiosity and autonomous thinking.

There’s still a large gap in common sense on the part of agentic AI for those of us hoping these tools will make our everyday lives outside of a 9-to-5 easier, more affordable or less hectic. I hope that changes as they learn.

#2995. Gen Z is the least interested in AI at work – and it’s not even close

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Younger workers don't find AI useful, according to a recent survey.

Generation Z might have the lowest morale around AI at work compared to other generations. That’s according to a survey from talent services firm Seramount, which found that Gen Z was the most AI-averse among the generations surveyed about using the technology in their jobs.

Gen Z, which includes those born between 1997 and 2012, expressed the least interest and found the least utility in AI, Seramount found. Only 18% of Gen Z reported an interest in strengthening their AI skills, compared to 36% of Millennials, 46% of Gen Xers, and 43% of Boomers. Gen Z is also using AI less than other generations, by nine percentage points.

Also: OpenAI is offering small businesses free AI support – and up to $8K/mo to experts who help them

“Employers cannot assume their youngest employees will embrace AI on their own,” said Diana Forster, senior director of research at Seramount.

The survey polled responses from over 1,800 US white-collar workers at companies with at least 500 employees.

Around half of Gen Z report weekly AI use (not specific to work), according to a survey from Walton Family Foundation, GSV Ventures and Gallup, but the generation’s skepticism has mounted over the past few years. Even members of Gen Z who use AI daily have less positive views on the technology. In the same study, 42% of Gen Z reported feeling anxious about AI in 2026, a 1% increase from 2025. Last year, 36% of Gen Z respondents reported excitement about AI. In 2026, that percentage dropped to 22%.

Also: These companies are actually upskilling their workers for AI – here’s how they do it

It’s no surprise Gen Z is skeptical about adopting a technology that could be undermining their own career development. The labor market has been particularly harsh to this group of workers, as entry-level job postings have fallen in recent years, and many fear that AI will only exacerbate unemployment. Around 8% of those ages 22 to 24 were unemployed in September, compared to 3% of workers ages 25 to 54, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

But with many workplaces still adopting AI, senior employees are trying to prepare Gen Z by getting them on board at work.

“We need to show young workers how AI can strengthen their work, provide clear guidelines and training, and give them opportunities to practice using it and build the skills they’ll need as leaders,” Forster said.

Our R&D expenses were RMB 425 million this quarter, up 4% year-on-year.

Excluding share-based compensation expenses, our adjusted R&D expenses increased by 6% year-on-year to RMB 350 million, mainly due to higher cloud service fees and server depreciation costs related to AI infrastructure investments. Our G&A expenses decreased by 34% year-on-year to RMB 241 million this quarter, mainly due to the one-off impairment of intangible assets recorded in the same period last year. Excluding the impairment, G&A expenses were relatively stable. Interest and investment recorded RMB 1.3 billion loss this quarter against RMB 228 million of income 1 year ago, mainly due to an approximately RMB 1.4 billion noncash fair value changes of one of our invested companies.

Income tax was a benefit of RMB 161 million this quarter compared with an expense of RMB 172 million a year ago. This shift reflects a noncash deferred tax benefit of RMB 361 million arising from the same investment loss described above, which more than offset our normal tax on operating profits. As a result, net income was a loss of RMB 249 million this quarter, driven by this noncash fair value adjustment. Despite the year-on-year growth in income from operations, excluding the above-mentioned investment loss, the related deferred tax benefit and share-based compensation expenses, adjusted net income was RMB 1.1 billion, up 12% year-on-year. Net cash provided by operating activities was RMB 1.3 billion this quarter.

As of June 30, 2026 (sic) [ September 30, 2026], our cash position, including cash, cash equivalents, short-term time deposits and short-term investments, both excluding -- but excluding investments in equity securities, stood at RMB 19.6 billion. Our strong cash position and cash-generating capability enable us to sustainably deliver our shareholder return commitment. As Jonathan just mentioned, today, our Board of Directors has authorized a new share repurchase program on top of the existing one, which effective from November 25, 2026, for a 12-month period, under which we may purchase additional up to USD 500 million of our shares, further reflecting the determination of the management to continue delivering shareholder return commitments.

And now for our business outlook, given the challenging recruitment demand trend for the fourth quarter of 2026, we expect our total revenues to be between RMB 2.19 billion and RMB 2.23 billion, a year-on-year increase of 5.3% to 7.3%. That concludes our prepared remarks. And now we would like to take -- answer questions. Operator, please go ahead.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] First question comes from the line of Timothy Zhao of Goldman Sachs.

Timothy Zhao: [Interpreted] It's a pleasure to see that we increased our shareholder commitment against this environment. I have 2 questions. One is, can management share what is the latest recruitment industry trend since third quarter this year to date? And what is the detailed trend by industry, by enterprise scale and by blue collar versus white collar? And secondly, could management elaborate how these changes reflect in your outlook in the fourth quarter revenue? And what is our observation on the market competitive landscape? And what is our solutions in order to grow the business in this environment?

Peng Zhao: [Interpreted] Thank you, Tim, for your question. So yes, we have observed that entering into the fourth quarter, the overall recruitment demand is challenging and especially the supply and demand situation, which showed more job seekers comparing to enterprise users, and this trend is still continuing. So this gives us quite a challenge to provide better service and satisfying service to more of our users. And if you look at details, so we saw that the change in magnitude from the small and medium-sized enterprises is bigger and also combined with the seasonality considerations because December is normally a low season.

So approaching the end of the year, the job seeker normally want to switch a job, and the recruiters were slowing down their recruiting activities. The bigger, larger companies performed the relatively more resilient because from 2 aspects: first, it will continue to finish its previous recruitment plan. So they still continue to do the recruiting activities. Another aspect is a lot of bigger enterprises will sign annual contract for the next year from October to December. So this signing activities is basically normal. From a blue and white collar perspective, the blue-collar users and revenue contribution further improved because we have better user growth and penetration among the blue-collar users.

And in the third quarter, the revenue contribution from blue-collar users increased by 1.5 percentage points year-on-year. One of noteworthy background here is that BOSS Zhipin was actually a white-collar-oriented platform from the beginning and in fact, but now we have gradually become more and more blue over these years. But the penetration rate of the whole blue-collar users are still on a fast-growing process. So we can understand this blue-collar penetration story will continue to drive our overall growth. From an industry perspective, the manufacturing industry continued to lead the growth.

In third quarter and the fourth quarter till today, the newly added job posting among manufacturing industry grew more than double digits year-on-year and the relatively lagging industries, including like automobile, finance, advertising and retail. So I understand this topic coming from the most concentrated concern of our company, which is growth. So actually, I have 3 wheels on our hand. The first one is in the lower-tier cities, we will continue the user penetration growth as our main engine.

And then in the other top-tier cities and some of the second-tier cities, the monetization reform, which main purpose is to reduce the escape and massive user complaints have achieved the initial success, so which enable us to further push forward this price reformation in the higher penetrated cities to increase our revenue growth. And the third one is a relatively smaller wheel, but it is also ongoing. So under the support of our technology, we are able to provide massive hiring -- fast massive hiring for bigger clients. So providing a very comprehensive service to deliver directly suitable candidates. This one is quite with strong certainty.

Another one is even smaller wheel, but we also see some silver lining that with the support of AI, we have provided very good service for our internal headhunter consultant to use undeveloped massive user resources to provide comprehensive service for complicated customers. So all these things are under normal operation. And back to the fourth quarter outlook, which you confirmed, given all those circumstances, we have a relatively cautious one. So from our historical pattern, we will deliver what we promised, and we will strive to even deliver better. So that's what we were working on. So to sum up, we are under different challenges, but still we have been optimistic for long term.

That's our answer for this question. And now, let's move on to the next one.

Operator: Next we have Eddy Wang from Morgan Stanley.

Eddy Wang: [Interpreted] During the prepared remarks, you mentioned that we have launched the pricing lift experiments in Beijing, Shanghai starting in the third quarter. Can you share more feedback from these recruiters? And how should we think about the pace of the future price increase and the impact on the long-term revenue growth? And the second question is, can you elaborate on the application of AI-enabled products and the closed-loop services? And what's the implication for our future pricing strategy and the revenue growth road map?

Peng Zhao: [Interpreted] I understand your concern about our customer reaction during our price reform in the first tier cities. This is the things we concern the most because our clients have paid money, paid time and patience. If he trusted this platform more, he also paid a cost of opportunity. My understanding is the customer is looking for a quick and -- quick candidates, which also suit him. So based on this understanding of our customers, now we are setting the price of our products on RMB 4 to RMB 6 per day in place like Beijing and Shanghai.

The meaning behind that, which means if I can give you 15 super candidates each month, then you are only paying us RMB 8 to RMB 12 for each super candidate. I think this is a very, very low price. So based on this judgment and understanding of the industry during our reform, we -- as we expected, there is no real user attrition, for example, more than 2% who showed that they will never use our platform again. So this is -- like this reform achieved success under our cautious control. In fact, we're also confident to invest more resources to better understand our clients who are still willing to hire.

But before they invest their time and patience and internal communications, we can better satisfy our clients, give them better results, so they were willing to pay us more for valuable service. Beijing is the first to accomplish this experiment, and we saw very positive results. And now we also finished our experiment for the first-tier cities. So we are confident that all this added together we will have positive impact and also another way to maybe to balance some of the lower season and impact -- external impact. And also about this AI, I just shared quite a lot during my remarks. But also currently, there are several things -- have definitely ongoing.

First, our client is using a lot of search function. So a lot of people are using search to do long text communication interaction so they can achieve better results from us. And some of very large clients use us like one-stop, we can call it a one-stop service, including assessing, communication and delivery. And this service is also going well. And also our internal consultant using our products to help them to better find candidates through our candidate pool to external people. All this together and including the price reformation we might perform in the second-tier cities and the products we have going out, all will gradually contribute to our business revenue growth next year.

And that's our answers to the second question. Let's move on to the next one.

Operator: Next, we have Wei Xiong from UBS.

Wei Xiong: [Interpreted] First, based on the current trends of high-end demand, what's our plan for investment in CapEx and other initiatives next year? And how should we think about the long-term margin level? And second, we noticed the new share repurchase program. So just wondering, could management share your thoughts around shareholder returns and payout ratio for next year?

Peng Zhao: [Interpreted] So thank you about our plan for investment. The first -- there are several directions. First is companies still want to try out our model to the country and district relatively friendly or more neutral to serve more clients and gain achievements. So that's one direction. The second is if some investment can further enhance our capability on matching recommendation, and also, our super price, who are willing to consider. So those 2 directions are quite clear. So one is on global and one is on recommendation. And on the CapEx front, we will focus more on our AI application.

But for the pretraining model investment, we will be constrained, and we definitely will not do any kind of competition of GPUs or [ matrix arms ]. And the margin, we will maintain relatively stable and may slightly increase and that can last longer term. Yes. And for the shareholder return on the payout ratio, so you can see we have very healthy and abundant cash reserve. We have overdelivered our promised 50% of shareholder return. At the beginning of this year, we actually did 100%. This USD 500 million new program, and also, we have some left. So together, we have almost USD 600 million total buyback quota over the next 12 months.

So we can expect the company will continue to overdeliver the shareholder return commitment and create value for our shareholders. And that's our answer to the third question. And given the time constraint, we can only take one last question, operator.

Operator: Next, we have Thomas Chong from Jefferies.

Thomas Chong: [Interpreted] Can management share about the progress for OfferToday and other overseas initiatives? What are our strategies entering the new market, the preliminary spending and KPI that can be shared?

Peng Zhao: [Interpreted] Thank you for your interest in OfferToday, which is our -- initially, it's actually an experiment in Hong Kong, China, but now we have -- find it, it actually went quite successful. From an app perspective, OfferToday -- online recruitment and job seeking app perspective, OfferToday have taken the #1 position in Hong Kong for quite a while. But it still take us longer term to learn how to use Cantonese, English and local slang to express information of job content and recruitment from excellent powerful local job seekers and local customers and grew alongside with us.

And another app also called OfferToday in the near future will also appear in Singapore, but it also will take a longer term to adapt how to better serve the local customers. And on our globalization, actually, we have a thinking matrix. That is we are willing to looking at one place or one city, whether they have a chance in 5 or in 10 years to realize the similar revenue size of -- which we see like Beijing and Hangzhou in 2 years. For example, Beijing, we are assuming they have like USD 150 million market size, Hangzhou maybe USD 100 million.

So if they have this kind of market potential, that's something which is worth spending time and money to invest. And on the other side of this metric is time. We simply divided into 5 years and 10 years 2 cycle. So if a 5-year investment, if we can see a similar size of Hangzhou, then we assume that's complying with our view on Hong Kong and -- China, Hong Kong and Singapore. And in fact, we find a lot of place who have -- or cities have similar opportunities, and we are willing to do similar investment. Also, last time I reported to you with a 5-year potential, and we call that middle dish.

And if a place takes 10 to 15 years' time to achieve similar scale, we're calling it like -- more like a slow dish. That's how we do it. We will document internally on how we'll invest our money and human resources. So I just fully shared with you the simple matrix. And that's all of our answers to today, and we can conclude today's call, operator.

Operator: Due to time constraints, that concludes today's Q&A session. At this time, I will turn the conference back to Laura for any additional or closing remarks.

Laura Zhan: Thank you once again for joining us today. If you have any further questions, please contact our IR team directly. Thank you. [Portions of this transcript that are marked [Interpreted] were spoken by an interpreter present on the live call.]

#2992. You can turn Claude artifacts into Windows and Mac apps now – here’s how

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Anthropic's new 'install as app' feature makes it easy to turn your Claude artifacts into desktop apps on your computer - with some limitations.

Anthropic is making its Claude artifacts available as desktop apps, meaning you can share and more easily access your most-repeated tasks on your computer. The “install as app” feature is available in beta for all free and paid Claude plans and works on both Mac and Windows, but not Linux.

Also: 4 ways Anthropic’s Claude Sheets beat using a Google Sheets connector

Anthropic first released artifacts in 2024. Since then, they’ve become a way to standardize and repeat tasks users do regularly, especially at work. Previously, artifacts ran via your Claude window or in a browser. By splicing them out as distinct desktop apps, you can now run different Claude queries while also using your artifacts locally, or use those apps without opening Claude at all.

“When an artifact is installed as a Mac or Windows app, it gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude. You can share it with others, and it needs your permission before it can interact with your computer,” Anthropic said.

Artifact apps can still access Claude and any connectors you’re using, and they update automatically when you edit the artifact itself in Claude. When apps request something from Claude, though, that goes toward your Claude usage limits, which are lowest for free users.

Anthropic said the app feature is meant to streamline building apps for both developer and non-developer work.

Also: Can AI plan terrorist attacks? US tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok

The update clarifies where AI software for work is headed. Claude is already more of an AI-powered work suite than a single helpful chatbot for many organizations. Evidently, people are using tools like artifacts frequently enough — and simultaneously with other Claude features — that they need those Claude-based tools to function like discrete bits of software on their own.

“If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention,” Anthropic said.

Claude artifact apps don’t have the same functionality as apps you could build using Claude Code, though. Even if you don’t need Claude open for these apps to work, you’ll still need to be signed in to Claude and have internet access, so they’re not an entirely portable or off-grid option.

The feature’s support page also notes that legacy artifacts, “live artifacts from Claude Cowork,” and artifacts generated from templates like Docs, Slides, and Sheets can’t be installed as desktop apps.

First, make sure Claude for Mac or Windows is updated. You can try the “install as app” feature, which is in beta for all free and paid plans, via Claude’s Share menu. Select the Install as app option, which will then download the artifact you chose to your desktop. From there, set permissions as needed.

Permissions range from the default (whatever they are in a browser) to app-specific permissions like sending notifications and full computer access.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a local AI stack that’s completely free

Full computer access means the artifact app can “run programs and read, change, or delete your files without asking each time,” Anthropic said, so proceed carefully. Every time you edit and update the artifact (and thus the app), Claude will ask you to confirm permissions again, so you’ll ideally have regular checkpoints to revise access. Still, there are some guardrails in place: Anthropic only lets you give full computer access to apps you’ve made yourself. For Team and Enterprise plans, that extends to any apps made by your coworkers.

“Anthropic doesn’t review apps before you install them, so only give full access to apps you trust,” the company said.

For Claude Enterprise plans, the install-as-app feature is off entirely until an admin turns it on in Organization settings.

#2991. What Is a Reconditioning Fee on a Used Car?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Used-car dealers may charge you a reconditioning fee to cover their costs of getting cars ready for sale.

A reconditioning fee is an added dealer charge you might find when buying a used car. It’s intended to cover any costs the dealer incurs to make sure a used car is showroom-ready, from mechanical inspections to detailing.

The reconditioning process varies between dealerships, but typically includes these steps:

A visual exterior inspection. An auto tech does a quick walk-around the vehicle and notes any corrosion, damage or wear.

An interior inspection. The engine and auto interior are examined and tested, and any issues are documented.

A test drive. The car is taken out for a drive to check that it runs well and that the radio, brakes, A/C and other components are all functioning properly.

Service and repair. Any interior or exterior mechanical, functional or cosmetic issues that were found are repaired, including paint, dents, oil changes and major engine work.

Inspection. Once repairs are completed, the car is inspected again to make sure everything looks and functions as it should.

Detailing. This includes deep interior, engine and exterior cleaning as well as any necessary leather refurbishing, bumper repair or wheel restoration.

Reconditioning fees are legal, but that doesn’t mean you have to pay them. Dealers can charge whatever they want for a reconditioning fee, and it’s not uncommon to find them ranging from around $500 to over $2,000.

The good news: Reconditioning fees, like most dealer extras, can be negotiable. Ask the dealer for a breakdown of the reconditioning fee to see what kind of work was done to prepare the car for sale. If the work was minor but the fee is high — for example, if they’re asking for $1,995 but replaced the floor mats only — that’s a good sign it’s a bogus charge.

However, when it comes time for negotiation, don’t just haggle over the reconditioning fee or other individual fees. The best way to negotiate is to focus on the out-the-door price, or the total amount you’re paying for the car. This simplifies the negotiation process and keeps you focused on the true price of your car.

All dealers invest some amount in reconditioning, but those costs are often built into the dealer’s asking price for a vehicle, rather than as a separate charge.

Some dealers opt to add a reconditioning fee to the bill because it allows them to advertise a lower asking price online, which doesn’t include fees. It’s a tactic to get you into their dealership, since the asking price is lower than that of other dealerships.

However, once you arrive, you may find that the out-the-door price is the same — or more — compared with what other dealers are asking.

Some car-buying experts recommend avoiding dealerships that charge reconditioning fees altogether. But remember that the out-the-door price is what matters at the end of the day, so it’s worth comparing prices at multiple dealerships to find the best deal.

Reddit is an online forum where users share their thoughts in “threads” on various topics. The popular site includes plenty of discussion on financial subjects like car buying, so we sifted through Reddit threads to get a sense of how users feel about reconditioning fees. People post anonymously, so we cannot confirm their individual experiences or circumstances.

Reddit users are generally skeptical toward reconditioning fees. Many users view these fees as a bait-and-switch tactic: dealers advertise an attractive price online and then tack on the fee at the dealership, inflating the actual out-the-door cost well above what was listed. Car buyers frequently share stories of being hit with reconditioning fees ranging from a few hundred dollars up to $2,000 or more, often with little or no evidence of what work was actually done.

Car-buying experts on Reddit point out that most dealerships already build reconditioning costs into the sticker price, so if the fee is listed separately, the dealership may be double-dipping. Several users suggest that car buyers ask their dealer for an itemized breakdown of the work done, but most users recommend negotiating the total out-the-door price rather than individual fees.

#2986. What Are Repositioning Cruises?

Repositioning cruises move ships between seasonal destinations, often with longer sailings, fewer port stops and lower fares.

A repositioning cruise is a one-way sailing that moves a ship from one region to another. For example, many ships sail in the Mediterranean Sea during the summer and move to the Caribbean Sea for the winter, and that trip between the two is a repositioning cruise.

Repositioning cruises are most common in spring (roughly March to May) and fall (roughly September to November), though they can occur at other times of year.

Because ships are crossing oceans, these trips often include many days at sea. For some travelers, that’s a chance to relax and enjoy the ship’s onboard amenities. Sometimes, these sailings can also be cheaper than traditional cruises.

One key consideration for a repositioning cruise is that the embarkation and disembarkation ports will be different. This means you generally can’t buy a standard round-trip flight to and from the same city. Instead, you’ll need transportation to where the cruise starts and another way home from where it ends, which usually means two one-way flights (or one open-jaw ticket) unless you live near one of the ports. While these one-way sailings may be more affordable than traditional cruises, airfare costs may be higher.

This could be a great opportunity to redeem miles for your flight.

Another feature that sets these cruises apart is that stops along the way tend to include ports that aren’t traditionally part of regular itineraries. These might include islands like Bermuda, the Azores or the Canary Islands, and on some northern routes, Greenland.

Just keep in mind that the main purpose of these sailings is to get to a new region for the next season’s itineraries rather than make daily port stops. So if you’re someone who wants to visit as many places as possible on a cruise, a repositioning sailing may not be the ideal choice.

Repositioning cruises are often longer than standard cruises, commonly running two to three weeks compared with about a week for a typical sailing, which may appeal to travelers looking for an extended vacation. The experience is often more relaxed, with many days at sea and less of a rush to book shore excursions or visit important sites when off the ship.

If there are particular ships with certain amenities — like tattoo parlors or massive waterparks — that you really want to experience, keep in mind that not all ships reposition between regions. Some stay in certain regions year-round.

For ships that do change locations for the season, there are plenty of onboard activities to fill the time. You can enjoy shows, food and wine tastings, organized activities and time at the spa, pool or casino.

Many repositioning crossings are relatively smooth, and modern ships use stabilizers to reduce movement. But since these itineraries cross open ocean rather than staying closer to land, there can be more motion, especially on North Atlantic crossings in fall and winter.

If you tend to get seasick, this could be a dealbreaker. Even if a repositioning sailing is smooth, temperatures can be chilly on the open ocean, especially on northerly or spring and fall transatlantic routes, with strong winds that may make suntanning by the pool less appealing.

You can book one of these sailings in the same way you would book a traditional cruise. But if you’re searching for dates and itineraries on a cruise line’s website, they may be listed as transatlantic, transpacific or Panama Canal sailings rather than repositioning cruises, though some lines do use the term "repositioning." There’s even a website that specializes in rounding up these cruises: RepoCruises.com.

Keep an eye out for themed sailings that focus on topics like wine, theater or music, where fellow guests on the ship may share similar interests. Cruise lines often schedule them on repositioning cruises to spur demand.

Here are some repositioning cruises for 2027. They often take place during shoulder seasons, between the most popular cruising times in places like the Mediterranean or Caribbean.

This journey repositions the ship from Miami, where it sails on Caribbean itineraries, to Seattle, where it will visit ports in Alaska during the spring and summer months. Departing April 8, 2027, the 18-night cruise includes stops at various ports in Colombia, Panama and Mexico, as well as San Diego and Los Angeles, before arriving in Seattle on April 26.

Regent Seven Seas Cruises' all-suite luxury ship Seven Seas Mariner will sail between New York and Lisbon, making stops in Canada, Morocco and the Portuguese islands of Madeira and the Azores.

Departing April 29, 2027, the 16-night journey ends in Lisbon, Portugal, as the ship repositions to Europe, where it will sail various itineraries, including Mediterranean sailings later in the summer season.

Departing Seattle on Sept. 28, 2027, Norwegian Jade will sail to Yokohama, Japan, with stops in Alaska and northern Japan. This is a way to travel across the Pacific with less jet lag, since the journey takes place over several days, with ship clocks typically adjusted gradually (often an hour at a time) during the sailing. Note that the voyage also crosses the International Date Line.

If Greenland has been on your bucket list, this 16-night sailing is a way to get up close and personal with its natural scenery. Departing Reykjavik on Aug. 25, 2027, Azamara Quest will sail from Iceland to the U.S. It will make stops in Greenland, Canada and New England before reaching the Big Apple.

Departing Bergen, Norway, on June 11, 2027, this 28-night sailing aboard Viking Vela sails around Iceland's coast, makes two stops in Greenland and crosses the Atlantic before reaching New York.
